speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
On what grounds were life and marine insurance companies ex-

eluded and fire insurance companies not
excluded?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Marine insurance companies have to compete with American companies in the lake and ocean carrying trade, and it was thought that the imposition of a tax would place them at a disadvantage, as their competitors would not be subject to this tax. I think the matter is of some importance, especially in connection with the trade upon the upper lakes, where there is keen competition between American and Canadian bottoms.
Do not our Canadian fire insurance companies have to compete with outside companies that come in here and take risks at a very much lower rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had a rather extensive discussion of this question last night, when I pointed out that these companies were not domiciled here and had not agents here. My hon. friend was absent last night, but he will see by Hansard that the matter was very fully discussed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
subtopic
speechtext: ['We had a rather extensive discussion of this question last night, when I pointed out that these companies were not domiciled here and had not agents here. My hon. friend was absent last night, but he will see by Hansard that the matter was very fully discussed.']

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My objection to this tax is that it is not upon the company, but upon the clients of the company. The company will of course pay the tax to the Government, but they will take care to charge it to their clients. I understand that telegraph and cable companies are doing a very profitable business, very profitable in every sense, and I think my hon. friend would do well to reverse his policy and tax the company instead of the senders of the messages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have given this matter very careful consideration. I think my right hon. friend will find that the profits of telegraph companies are not large. They have to compete with telephone companies, and perhaps my right hon. friend had in mind that telephone companies should also be directly taxed; but the difficulty that arises in connection with directly taxing

telephone companies is that there are, as my right hon. friend knows, joint stock telephone companies doing business in Canada which have franchises and privileges from this Government or from other Governments. There are also co-operative telephone companies to compete with, and, in addition to that, Government-owned telephone systems. I considered very carefully the imposition of a tax upon telephone companies, v.ut when I pursued the matter I found myself brought up against the co-operative telephone companies and the Government-owned telephones in the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. It appeared to me that it would be unwise, even if we had the power, which I very much doubt, for the Government to tax the Government-owned telephone systems in the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan; and after a very full consideration of the whole question we reached the conclusion that we could not properly tax the telephone companies. Any legislation of that kind should be general in character, and not aimed at one or two individual companies. Speaking generally, those who use the telephone and the telegraph are the well-to-do members of the community; there are exceptions, of course, but what we had in mind was the levying of the tax upon those of the population who might reasonably be expected to contribute to this war taxation. Under the circumstances, therefore, we imposed the tax, as my hon. friend has said, upon the sender of the message.
There is another consideration that I am sure will appeal to my right hon. friend. The question of tolls Charged by telegraph and cable companies has been very frequently discussed in this House, and it is one of great concern to the commercial community. For reasons that it is not necessary to go into here, as they have been so often put forward in this House, I think it is extremely advisable that our cable tolls should be as low as possible,
How much do you expect from this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We calculated, but it is only an estimate, to receive something in excess of $100,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I must say that I am not thoroughly convinced, and for the good reason that my hon. friend has been discussing telephone, not telegraph, companies. The two things are very different, but I will take up what my hon.

friend has said about telephone companies.
I would not suggest that we should tax the * Government telephone systems. I would doubt our authority to do that, though I believe we might find authority. Government telephones were established because it was supposed that the tolls of the telephone companies were too high, and that a better service, or at all events a cheaper service, could be given by the governments. I understand that the experiment has not been a very great success in some parts of the country where it has been tried, and I do not for a moment suggest that we should tax the government telephones or the .co-operative telephones either. But let us come to the concrete fact that there are telephone companies in Canada; and there is reason to believe, I .may say it is a well-known fact that some of them, and I think all of them, are very successful. Their stock is one of the best that can be had on the market to-day, and I see no reason why under the present circumstances these companies should not be subjected to the imposition of the taxation which is being placed upon every citizen. It is expected that under this tariff, which is a war tariff, every citizen shall contribute his quota to the undertakings we have in mind. I cannot see any good reason why the powerful companies which I have just mentioned should not pay their share the .same as any other member of the commuity, and I believe my hen. friend would have been well advised if he had brought these companies under the operation of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After all, these companies are owned by their shareholders. Their shareholders are subject to this taxation because they will pay the tax, just as other citizens will, in the telegraph and cable messages which they send.

They do not pay it as
shareholders.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not as shareholders.
Those who are not shareholders pay the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree, but they are shareholders of the company and they will pay their share of the tax in the telegrams and cables that they send. I do not agree with my hon. friend that there are many telephone companies that are doing well in Canada. The Bell Telephone Company is a fairly strong institution, and probably! that is the company that my hon. friend had in mind. My view is that tolls imposed
directly upon public service corporations will be shifted upon the public. Having regard to considerations of that character, namely, the existence of co-operative companies and of government systems, which in competition with the telephone companies have had their effect upon tolls, it occurred to me that it would be invidious to select one company and impose a special tax upon it and not deal with the telephone or telegraph companies as a class. When I am framing legislation I like to deal with a class and if I find I cannot deal with a class I feel reluctant to proceed with the measure. If you pursue such a course you select from a class one, two, or more, and impose your tax upon them. This tax seems to me to be a very reasonable tax which will fall upon a body of citizens who are well able to pay it-business houses, commercial firms, railway companies and individuals who are comparatively well-to-do-and who can afford to pay this comparatively small tax upon telegraph messages and cables.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN-What is the gross income of the two leading telegraph systems in Canada-the Western Union and the Great Northwestern, which are looked upon as one-I may not be correct in that-and the Canadian Pacific railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am unable to give my
hon. friend that information.

Would it not have been just as fair to have taxed the income of telegraph companies at such a rate as would yield the $100,000 that the minister anticipates getting from this source as to levy a tax of one per cent upon the gross income of loan and trust companies as provided in clause 2 of the resolutions? It is the same principle and I would have thought that it would have been a very good principle indeed to have applied to the telegraph companies. I think they might very well pay that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree with my
lion, friend. I think there is a clear differentiation between the case of financial companies and that of companies such as we arc now considering. We make the companies our collectors of the tax. I do not desire to go over 'he argument, that 1 have aiready advanced as to the competi-tl .n which these o ninecies meet. It is not true in the case of financial institutions, i or it is true to a very limited extent. It
Imay be true as far as the post office savings are concerned but in practice there is no active competition to be met by finan-

cial companies while there is a very active competition prevailing with respect to telephone companies.

I am eliminating the
telephone companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well then the telegraph
is in competition with the telephone. Telegraph companies have complained to me that we have not taxed telephone messages.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend says " of course." There is a great deal of wisdom in that remark because we all like to have the taxes put over on the other man. That is human but I have to hold the scales of justice as fairly as I can.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is what my hon. friend does not do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend, if
he were less biased, would see that I have held them very evenly. My right hon. friend should know that justice is blind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I see that
now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend suggest that he is blind? He is blind to the merits of the proposals that .this Government bring forward. There have been complaints made to me that we have placed a tax upon telegrams and not upon telephone messages. I considered the question of placing a tax on telephone messages but I encountered the government-owned and co-operative telephone companies throughout the country. I considered a wide range of companies for the application of this tax but I found difficulties in connection with a great many that I should very much liked to have taxed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend has given a very good reason why this whole attempt at taxation is wrong. Instead of placing his tax upon telegraph companies he places it upon the clients of the companies and he says that it will not weigh very heavily upon the clients of these companies at all but that it will be paid by the wealthy corporations, the railway companies, mercantile firms and other firms of that kind. It is very true that they are chiefly the clients of the telegraph companies but if these parties have to submit to taxation why not the telegraph companies also who are wealthy companies? It would have been fairer to have placed the tax upon the companies themselves. If you have a

tax it should be placed upon the stock of the company and not upon the clients of the company.

We find that the Minister of Finance proceeds in regard to the tax on railway tickets along the same lines. He will not tax the railway company but he is going to tax the individual, the man who buys the ticket, and he is going to tax the man who sends the telegram. That is the whole trouble with my hon. friend. He wants to exempt these corporations. He says that railway companies, telegraph companies and telephone companies should not be taxed but that if there is any tax to be paid at all it ought to be paid by the people who use these services. The minister says they are quite able to pay. That is true if that were the only burden placed upon them but, under this measure, they have to pay an increased tariff upon what they wear, upon their clothing, upon practically everything they use, if they travel on the railway they have to pay the extra tax upon their railway ticket, if they send a telegram they have to pay the extra tax on the telegram, and the result is that you are going to burden the common people, the mass of the people, with this tax to such an extent that if they want to live at all they will have to get down to a pretty low diet-something like the Germans, pancakes, potatoes and buttermilk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And squid.
When my hon. friend, being filled with glory, departs from this life there will be found graven on his heart the word "squid."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned I am going to declare a truce between my hon. friend from St. John and myself on the word "squid." We all make an occasional mistake and it should not be magnified. I have always had a great deal of admiration for the control which my hon. friend is able to exert upon his countenance, but I do not know that his features were ever so impassive as they were when he made the statement that this measure relieved the large corporations and placed the entire burden upon the common people. My hon. friend spoke in regard to the railways. He knows to what extent the railways of Canada, with one exception, are capable at this particular time of bearing a heavy load of taxation.
My hon. friend also knows, because it would not escape his observation, that we are im-

posing an exceedingly heavy tax upon the railways of Canada by our measure as a whole. If he will take the trouble to look into it, he will ascertain that the Canadian railways will pay no less a sum than $1,000,000 a year-I think $1,250,000-in increased duties upon coal. The charges upon their administrative offices in connection with the war stamp taxation upon letters will run into very large sums. I do not desire to elaborate that point too greatly here, but the railways of Canada have certainly not been overlooked in this taxation measure.
My right hon. friend has said that the banks have come off very easily. I would point out to him that a taxation measure, imposing a yearly tax of $150,000 on the Bank of Montreal, $135,000 on the Bank of Commerce, and $60,000 on the Imperial Bank, and proportionate amounts on the other banks, can hardly be regarded as a measure not imposing heavy taxation upon those institutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Big amounts, but only one per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One per cent seems small, but the total amount is large, and my right hon. friend must remember that it is an annual charge. If my right hon. friend, during his term of office, had been of the view that the banks could well stand a higher rate of taxation than one per cent upon note circulation in return for the privilege of note circulation, he would not have hesitated to employ that method of raising money unless he felt unduly tender towards those institutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are breaking new
ground.

My hon. friend speaks about taxing the banks one per cent. Take the ordinary people of this country. Does not my hon. friend think they would be well satisfied if their taxation did not amount to more than one per cent of their income? The ordinary man with an income of $1,000 a year would be glad to get off with a tax of only $10. His share must be more than that, owing to the extra tax on food and clothing, and still more if he burns soft coal for heating his house, as many people do. In the town of Campbellton, N.B., hardly a ton of hard coal is used. People burning soft coal have to bear the increased duty just as much as the railway companies.
My hon. friend says that some railway companies will pay a tax of $1,000,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The three railways together.
I suppose the total income of the three railways would be about $150,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much net income?

I am speaking of the
total income. Very few of us have a net income. The ordinary man earning $1,000 a year has not very much left by the time he has paid out the various expenses incident to his living. If he makes ends meet by the end of the year, he has done well. The Minister of Finance is trying to single out the corporations for exemption. He has no regard for the mass of the people of this country; he puts the tax upon them without any apology at all. He does not endeavour to show how they can be exempted; but when it comes to great corporations, with a total income of $150,000,000 a year, he points out how heavily they are taxed. Take the Bell Telephone Company, which has for years paid a dividend of 8 per cent, and which is one of the strongest institutions m this country, operating in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and having a monopoly in cities like Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All taxed.

It is certainly a monopoly, because there are no other companies competing with it to any extent. My hon. friend does not propose to put any tax at all upon that company. Take the Western Union and the Great Northwestern Telegraph Companies. The Western Union has an enormous capital. My hon. friend does not propose to make those companies contribute one cent of this tax; but if a poor man sends a telegram he has to bear the burden and pay the extra toll.
Take the street railways in Montreal, Toronto and all the other great cities of Canada. Are they not to contribute out of their handsome profits? Not one cent is imposed upon them. If it were of any use at this late hour, I would urge my hon. friend to impose a tax upon them, but he would say: Oh, see the burdens that those street railway companies have to bear. He forgets that those street railways carry hundreds of thousands of people every day, and that their incomes are enormous. If my hon. friend had considered ways and means

of getting a reasonable tax out of those wealthy corporations, he would have done much better than he has by imposing a tax upon the mass of the people who are least able to bear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend speaks of t|he great incomes of the railway corporations, but let me put the question to him fairly. In dealing with taxation measures, we have to deal with classes; we have to deal with institutions belonging to a class as a whole. We can not single out for special taxation a wealthy corporation or Individual, and pass over those less wealthy of the same class. How much taxation would the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company be able to stand to-day? My hon. friend says that the average citizen has to pay more for his coal; the railway companies, as I have pointed out, have to pay more for their coal. The banks will be subject to nearly all those taxes which are imposed in our fiscal measure, either by Themselves as institutions or by their shareholders who are the proprietors.
I understand that the banks all heat their buildings with hard coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have levied a special tax upon the banks. My hon. friend knows, because his mind is too clear and he is too able a man not to know, that there is only one railway company in Canada able to sustain the burden of heavy federal taxation. He asks why 1 did not turn my mind to the question of street railway companies. I did consider that question. In Canada there are three or four street railway companies of a local character that might fairly have been made subject to this taxation; but the Dominion Government must not occupy the entire field of taxation. I want to leave something for the provinces. The provinces have to face the situation created 'by the war, and it was the object of the Government not to pre-empt or occupy the entire field to obtain a comparatively small amount from the half-dozen or less street railway companies in Canada. It seemed better to us that the Dominion Government in its legislation relating to taxation should take a broader sweep and deal only with those institutions and organizations and companies that are carrying on a Dominion business, and that it should leave something for the provinces, because it is increasingly apparent to me that the war has brought them almost as difficult 
problems as those with which the Dominion has had to grapple. I do net believe it would have been proper for the Government to have invaded the field of the provinces by imposing special taxes, say, upon picture-shows, theatres, and surface railways. I wish to leave those for the provinces, and I think it is sound policy.

Do not the masses of the people have to bear their burden of provincial taxation already? Why does not he leave the field so far as they also are concerned to the provincial governments and the municipalities? This is an extra tax by reason of existing conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's question is very easily answered. The provinces do tax the ordinary man for municipal and provincial purposes, just as the Dominion taxes the ordinary man through its fiscal system. What I had reference to was special taxation necessitated by the outbreak of this war, and I said it was advisable, in my opinion, that we should leave something of a special character for the provinces, which have to meet almost the same conditions as those with which we are confronted as the result of the outbreak of the war. I think there would have been complaints from one end of Canada to the other if the Dominion Government had invaded the field of the provinces and imposed a tax in addition to the tax, say, which the province of Quebec has recently imposed upon purely local undertakings. We must have some regard to provincial rights and necessities at a time such as this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I fail to see what connection there is between this kind of taxation and the provincial taxation. My hon. friend gave as a reason why he should not tax the large corporations, railways for instance, that one railway could have borne additional taxation. I have no doubt whatever that some of the railway companies, perhaps all but one, would have had some difliculty in meeting extra taxation; but does the hon. gentleman contend that the new taxation he is imposing on individuals will be met without difficulty? The same thing that applies to a corporation applies to an individual. There are hundreds of thousands of individuals who find themselves in the same circumstances as the Grand Trunk railway or any other corporation. The hon. gentleman argued strongly to prove that all classes should bear their share of the taxation. It is no answer to that to say that one class should not be called upon to bear its share of the taxa-

tion because it would find it difficult to pay. If that is what the hon. gentleman thinks, better wipe out this taxation altogether, for he knows as well as I do that many an individual called upon to bear this extra taxation will find it just as difficult to pay this ten dollars as the Grand Trunk railway would find it to pay half a million.

If I see the point that the minister tries to make, I think there is something in his contention, especially as he supports it by citing the well-known fact that there is only one railway company in Canada that is earning a Teal income. He makes a distinction which I think ought to be made between the gross takings of a corporation and the actual income of that corporation. I think there is a great deal in that contention. But he can hardly expect me to point that out without going on to say that that very contention, supported by that fact, makes it obvious that for the taxing of these corporations the income tax would have had very great advantages. He contends that a tax upon gross takings would be an injustice to the corporation which in spite of its gross takings does not have an income. It follows equally-does it not,-that leaving incomes untaxed is something of a favour to the wealthy corporations that do have incomes. Clearly, the income tax would have caught the wealthy corporations and, quite properly, would have allowed those to escape that have no income. I am sure he will not think I am trying to hold up the work of the committee if I take the time to score a little point in favour of the form of taxation that I proposed in the course of the Budget debate.

I desire to read from this morning's Citizen something abouts the earnings of the telegraph companies :
The report of the comptroller of statistics, Mr. J. I.. Payne, shows that on a total capitalization of $7,100,000 gross earnings of the various companies were $5,983,204 and operating expenses $4,242,539.
Here is an excess of earnings over expenses of $1,740,665.
The Canadian Pacific railway telegraph earned $2,991,273, the Great Northwestern, $1,252,930; Western Union (Canada) $668,252; Canadian Northern $264,615 and Marconi Wireless $239,906. Land messages numbered 11,980,869 and cables 983,061.
One cent each on the total number of messages I have quoted would give the revenue the minister anticipates.

If the income tax could be easily collected and without great expense I should certainly be in favour of it. I know something about it because my sessional indemnity was assessed some years ago and I fought the assessment, but the court held that my indemnity was assessable, and I have been paying taxes on it ever since. I think the income tax is a just tax, and all those that get sufficient income to enable them to pay ought to be made to pay. The great disadvantage that I see in it is that the minister would have to appoint a large number of collectors, and God knows there are enough civil servants already. Perhaps he could use a large number of those who are in the employ of his colleague the Minister of Inland Revenue, who are getting reasonable salaries and have nothing, or almost nothing, to do. The other night some hon. members from the maritime provinces told us that they had in their counties officers receiving from $200 to $400 a year who have nothing to do, and these could be easily employed in collecting the income tax. An income tax was imposed in the United States a few years ago on salaries over $3,000. I do not think there could be any injustice if men were taxed on income in excess of $3,000. In Ontario the municipal income tax reaches salaries over $1,200 in municipalities under 10,000 population an $$1,500 in municipalities of over 10,000 population. I think it is only just that persons who receive an income of more than $2,000 should pay a tax upon it for Federal purposes.

Will the Government have to pay this one-cent toll on their
messages?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No statute applies to the Crown unless it is specially so provided.

speakerposition: stagedirection
stagedirection
subtopic
speechtext: ['No statute applies to the Crown unless it is specially so provided.']
If the minister will permit me to ask a question with regard to section 1, may I inquire if he is aware that the banks will shift the tax placed upon them to the shoulders of their customers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not aware that that will occur. On the contrary, I have received letters from banks stating that they will be glad to pay the tax, and to pay it themselves. I do not believe the payment of the tax will be shifted.

I have received a letter from a wholesale house in Montreal stating that the rate of discount on commercial papers has been raised by a certain bank. In this way they will take the amount of the tax from their customers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think that that
is a case of post hoc, ergo propter hoc.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Everybody who can shift this tax to somebody else will surely do so; that is human nature. I protested some days ago against this method of levying a tax on railway tickets; I shall not now repeat my objection. I should like to have an explanation as to why this tax is limited to certain classes of travel. This provision includes the following paragraph:
A ticket or right entitling the purchaser to transportation by vessel between ports or places in Canada or from a port or place in Canada to a port or place in Newfoundland, the West Indies, Bermuda, British Guiana, British Honduras or the United States.
Nothing is collected from passengers on steamers which are leaving every week for Great Britain and for European ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is covered in the next section.

Would it not be much better to impose a tax of one per cent on the value of every ticket purchased? A person who buys a first-class ticket at $2 pays the same tax as a person who buys a first-class ticket at $4.99. Those who buy first-class tickets are probably better able to pay the tax; they consist of agents of wholesale houses, etc. The tax wb;"b the

' minister proposes is virtually a one per cent tax upon tickets costing from $1 to $5. If one per cent were the basis, a person buying a ticket costing $1 would pay one cent, and a person buying a ticket costing $4 would pay four cents; there would be a uniform basis of some kind. I direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the poorer people do not often travel far, and do not pay high prices for tickets. ~

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
recognize that we must fix a point in respect of which a certain rate shall apply. We have fixed upon one dollar, we have said that with regard to tickets that cost less than one dollar there shall be no taxation, but upon tickets costing from one dollar to five dollars, five cents must be paid. That means that there is a maximum taxation of 5 per cent and a minimum taxation of one per cent. As between the poor man who travels but little and the ordinary citizen or the wealthy man who travels much, my hon. friend will bear in mind the fact that every time a person travels he must pay a tax. The representatives of wholesale houses, therefore, to whom my hon. friend has referred, and persons who travel considerably and can afford to do so, will have to pay the tax very many more times than those who travel but little. Again, wealthy members of the community, generally speaking, travel longer distances, therefore will have to pay more, because the tax increases as the price of the ticket increases. It was suggested to me-I do not propose to argue the matter at length-that a much larger tax should be imposed for the greater distances. We gave that matter -which affects also the tax upon parlour car seats and sleeping berths-very careful consideration. It must be remembered that our Canadian railways are in competition with the American roads and that, owing to the geographical position of Canada, it is quite possible to go from one part of Canada to another, especially to a remote part, by going through the United States. If, therefore, I imposed an unduly heavy tax upon tickets for the longer distances, people living say in Toronto, Montreal, Chatham, Windsor-especially in cities near the border-would buy their tickets in the United States and go via the United States for the greater part of their journey. Having regard to all these considerations, we reached the conclusion that the tax should be comparatively small and uniform, so the burden should fall upon that part of the community most capable of bearing it. As

a rule, the persons who travel the greater distances and the more frequently are better able to pay than those who travel but little.
If a person buys a book ef commutation tickets, will he pay the tax when he buys the book or when the coupons are collected on the train?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He will have to pay when he buys but my hon. friend will remember that there is a dollar of exemption.*

Has the minister
thought about the great number of people who travel through the country on passes and who could well afford to pay a tax?
Only members of Parliament.

I know there are more than members of Parliament. I was in a car recently and there were at least twenty-five of us and only two had tickets. It seems to me that those who were in the car could well afford to pay the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, I am
afraid, is really trespassing on dangerous ground in reference to one of the most sacred privileges of the members of this House.
That makes no difference, they can afford to pay better than the poor man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If every hon. gentleman
starts to his feet at once and says he would be very glad if the Government would take into consideration a comprehensive plan of taxation whereby every time he uses his pass, which is his by virtue of statutory law, he would pay a substantial tax I would not say that we would at once move that the idea be translated into legislation but I can promise that I would take it into my most serious consideration.
And private passes and private cars also?
I mean all passes, the members of this House can as well afford to pay a tax as any one else. I am willing to do it and I do not see why it is not done.
Do I understand the minister to say that there will be no special taxes on railway passes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The passenger must be the purchaser of a ticket before the tax applies, otherwise I do not think it could be enforced.
This provision exempts not only passes but private cars as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has referred much more frequently to private cars since he has occupied a seat on that side of the House than he is reported in Hansard as having referred to them during the entire period of his occupation of a seat on this side of the House.
When I was a minister under the last Government the number of private cars available for the ministers was very much fewer than it is under this Government

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend used to
charter a private car in the United States when he wanted one.

Only on two occasions when I went to the West in my capacity as Minister of Public Works. I notice now that if a minister wants to go to St. John or to Montreal or to Toronto he has a private car. Nothing of the kind existed in the days of the Liberal Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the days of old.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6:
That every purchaser of a berth in a sleeping car or seat in a parlour car shall, in addition to the regular charge for the berth or seat, pay to the person selling the berth or seat for the Consolidated Revenue Fund-
(a)	ten cents in respect of each berth bought:
(b)	five cents in respect of each seat bought;

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['In the days of old.']

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What will be the tax in the case of long distance travelling, say if a man buys a pullman ticket from Ottawa to Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What would be the tax paid by the traveller who leaves Ottawa for Winnipeg and who has a pullman ticket that entitles him to a seat in the day time and a berth at night? How 1 much would he pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He would pay 10 cents in respect of each berth and 5 cents in respect of each seat. If the berth gave the right to a seat in the day time the whole tax would be 10 cents. We must have regard, in considering this legislation, to the condition of travel that actually exists. I pointed out that this tax, instead of being a light tax, was really a very heavy tax.
A passenger, a citizen of Toronto, is proceeding to Hamilton. He takes a seat in

the parlour ear. The charge for that to-day is 25 cents. He will now pay 30 cents. That is to say, we have taxed him 20 per cent, or one-fifth of the amount. It is true that for long distances, say from Montreal to Winnipeg or Vancouver, the same rate applies; but as I pointed out, the travelling public are those who travel frequently and the tax will average up well and be a very substantial tax upon that part of the community, the travelling men, who are usually quite able to pay the tax. There is further consideration that I mentioned when discussing the former section that if we increased this rate beyond a certain point the passenger at Windsor or other border points would simply purchase a ticket to Detroit and there buy his sleeping car accommodation and parlour car accommodation through the United States to the boundary of Canada on his way to Winnipeg or Vancouver. That would result in a discrimination against Canadian railways. We have given full consideration to the matter and I believe the conclusion we have reached is wise.
That would only apply to the border towns like Detroit where they could cross over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many border towns.
Does a traveller pay only 10 cents for his pullman going to Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It seems to me that the whole system is really a discrimination against the poorer travellers. Here are two men going from Ottawa to Montreal. One man takes a first-class ticket and pays $3.35. The other man takes a second-class ticket and pays $2.75. They both pay 5 cents tax, the poor man pays just as much as the wealthy man. It seems to me that there should be a graduation. My hon. friend has considered only the distance, but the very essence of our travelling system is that there is a difference in the prices to be paid. There is a price for the poor man and a price for the wealthy man. That is why there are two classes of railway carriages, simply because the poor man cannot afford to pay as much as the wealthy man; but yet you make him pay the same amount of taxation upon his ticket. Take a man who goes to Toronto. He pays from Ottawa to Toronto, firstrclass, $7.70, and second-class $6.40. On both 
classes of ticket the tax will be 10 cents. The poor man will pay as much as the wealthy man. There is no justice in that, and the graduation should be as I suggested.
A man goes from Ottawa to Winnipeg. He pays for his first-class fare $34.70. Another man, travelling second-class, pays $26.50. One will pay 30 cents and the other 25 cents, a difference of only 5 cents in taxation for that immense distance. Moreover, the man who travels first-class will probably take a pullman car, for which he pays $7.75 from Ottawa to Winnipeg, and he will pay on that pullman ticket only 10 cents of taxation. It seems to me that the whole thing is inconsistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend has chosen just those instances that fit his argument. Take the case of a first-class ticket that costs $1 or $1.10; a second-class ticket for the same distance would cost under a dollar; what happens there? Just let me turn the argument on my right hon. friend. The poor man pays nothing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no fault to find with it; we intended that that should be so; but the man who buys a first-class ticket costing over a dollar pays 5 cents. Take another case. How much would the man have to pay who buys a second class ticket costing under $5, say $4.75, $4.80 or $4.90? He pays 5 cents. Suppose the first class ticket is $5.50; how much does that man pay? He pays 10 cents, just double. Of course if my right hon. friend takes only those cases that happen to be inside the five dollar unit, he will appear to prove his case. But he has entirely failed to take into consideration the equally large number of cases in which the first-class traveller will, as compared with the second-class traveller, pay double when the second-class ticket is just under five dollars. My right hon. friend made another point, and he made it the other day too. He took the case of a poor man buying a second-class ticket from Ottawa to Montreal. It was quite a picture that he painted of the youthful 5 p.m. scion of wealthy parents lolling in luxury and paying only 5 cents for his seat; but my right hon. friend failed to point out that the man in the parlour car pays a tax upon his ordinary railway ticket, which would be first class, and, as I have shown, the tax might be considerably in excess of what the man with the second-class ticket would have to pay. The man with the first-class ticket pays not only

the extra 25 or 50 cents, which is the normal charge for a seat in the parlour car, but five cents as well; and it is proper that he should.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have done even-handed
justice between the man who buys a first-class ticket and a seat in the parlour car, and those less fortunate members of the community who cannot afford that. My right hon. friend always travels in the parlour car and I should not like to see him travel in anything but a parlour car. But there is this further consideration, and I submit that this whole question cannot be discussed unless we have regard to it all the time. Nothing would please me better than to impose a larger tax according to distance; that occurred to me at the outset, just as it did to my right hon. friend. It is revenue that I want, and if I could get a larger revenue by imposing a higher tax between Toronto and Vancouver, I should be delighted to do it. But we must bear in mind two things: first, if you increase the tax unduly you will discourage travelling; and secondly, if you impose a substantial tax according to distance, you will divert to the United States the travel which should go over Canadian lines; and I have not in mind advantage to Canadian railway lines only, but to the Canadian public as well. Having regard to all these considerations, and to the conditions that exist in Canada, which has a boundary line of practically four thousand miles separating us from the United States, which has a network of railway lines leading up to our border, I think this taxation is fair and just and necessary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not object to the tax; I think it is fair enough if we have to have a war tax. But what I do object to is the basis upon which it is founded. My hon. friend has completely ignored the basis upon which we travel; that is, that there are two classes of travel, and therefore two different prices. My hon. friend has put them exactly on the same footing, and that is the fault I have tried to find. My hon. friend says that I travel in the pullman car.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope you do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My poor
means permit me to pay for that, hut it seems to me that if I want to enjoy the luxury of travelling in a pullman car and 76
can afford to do so, I should be called upon to pay more than the poor man who cannot travel in the pullman. The man who goes in a pullman car from here to Montreal is charged only 5 cents, when that very man would give more as a tip to the nigger who attends on him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend says that his poor means enable him to travel in the pullman car Now, if I imposed an undue tax I should perhaps be depriving him of that privilege, for he might not be able to afford it. There is another point. If I increase this tax beyond 5 cents, the porter may be deprived of that tip which is his by immemorial right, and the Government of Canada would be enriching itself at the expense of one of the most deserving classes in the community. I must bear all these things in mind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.
The companies could pay their porters.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7:
That every purchaser of a ticket or right entitling the purchaser, either with or without intervening transportation, to transportation by vessel from a port or place either in or outside of Canada to a port or place outside of Canada other than in Newfoundland, the West Indies, Bermuda, British Guiana, British Honduras or the United States shall, in addition to the regular ohargi for the ticket or right, pay in respect of the transportation by vessel to the person selling the ticket or right for the Consolidated Revenue Fund

speakerposition: stagedirection
subtopic
speechtext: ['The companies could pay their porters.']
This will be a very heavy tax on those going home third-class to visit their parents in the old country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, I think not. As the
resolutions were brought down originally the rates were fixed on the same basis as the rates out of American ports. Of course, if the tax upon these tickets brought the Canadian rate higher than the American rate, we should divert to American ports the travel which now goes from our own ports. The tax is fairly heavy, but the total amount we expect to get is comparatively small, probably $15,000 or $20,000. That is not a very large amount. As my



hon. friend will see we have made a differentiation : the sum of one dollar is charged -if the transportation exceeds $10, and $3 if it exceeds $40. We understand that the second-class passages are below $40, so in section (b) we made it $40 instead of $30, so as to make the tax less in proportion for those buying tickets under $40. The railway tax is a very small one, a five cent tax so to speak; but this tax is larger. The total amount that will be collected, however, will not be very much, and on the whole I think this proposal may be regarded as very fair.
Take those who travel steerage. The price of a ticket to the old country is $33.50, I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One dollar.
The first and second class will pay more?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends upon the cost.
The second-class fare is $52.50.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the tax will be $3.
The steerage will not be any more?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One dollar.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How much do you expect from this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimate is low, $15,000, but I think it may be more. It is a small tax and the question might almost arise whether it is worth while.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think that estimate is too low.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is too low; I think it will be more.
Will it be collected from those who travel on Government steamers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
8. That no person shall issue a cheque payable at or by a bank unless there is affixed thereto an adhesive stamp, or unless there is impressed thereon by mean of a die, a stamp of the value of two cents ;

speakerposition: subtopic
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How much is expected from that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From cheques, bills of exchange and promissory notes I expect to receive $600,000. I do not believe it is possible to make an accurate estimate

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is one of the things in regard to which I would have supposed that the calculation would be very accurate because every bank knows how many cheques pass through its hands every year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The difficulty is that so
many cheques and drafts pass between the branches of the banks themselves. I do not believe they are kept separate as to number. At all events, the estimate I have is about $600,000.
In estimating the amount the minister expects to derive from this tax, has he taken into consideration the amount that has been passing through the banks during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no accurate information and this is only an estimate. My officers made certain inquiries but we have not before us the facts upon which an accurate computation can be made. I understand it is not possible to obtain it from any of the returns.

I would think that probably large firms who have hitherto been paying by cheque might draw one large cheque and pay out currency. In that event the revenue would be very much less than the minister thinks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite possible. I should think that, in regard to the very small cheques issued by business houses, they might not issue so many as they have in the past. They might draw a cheque and disburse the currency. On the other hand, the tax is comparatively small, and the inconvenience, not to say the danger of keeping on hand large sums of money, would, I think, be such that the tax would not be likely to restrain companies or firms from carrying on business in the same way as they have in the past, or practically so.

May I call the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) to the experience of Germany with regard to a tax on cheques? In 1913, when Germany had to revise and modify her whole system of taxation as the result of her enormous increase in her naval and military expenditure, they enacted four laws. One was to modify the financial system of the Empire and to provide for an increase in the war fund; the second was to provide for the levying of what was called a special and extraordinary military contribution; the third was to impose a tax on

the increase of private fortunes having reference to both income and capital, and the fourth, which is the one that I want especially to draw the attention of the minister to, was a modification of the stamp tax. They repealed altogether the stamp tax on cheques which had been imposed in 1909. They did it because experience had shown that they derived from it the very insignificant revenue of 3,000,000 marks, equal to about $750,000. It was found to be an impediment to business and a great restriction on the normal development of circulation. They repealed it altogether while increasing all other forms of taxation. I think the Minister of Finance ought to be guided by the experience of Germany in that regard because there is no country that has had to levy taxes on account of military expenditure as Germany has had to do during the last few years, and especially after the speech of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) who, I am sure, would second my view in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that a tax of this kind is not likely to be an impediment to trade because a stamp tax has been in vogue in Great Britain, which is the greatest commercial country in the world, and it has probably very many more transactions in cheques than Germany has. As far as I can ascertain there is no likelihood of their changing that system. There is also a system of stamp taxes upon cheques in the United States. Whether it is in existence to-day or not I do not know, but it was during the Spanish-American war. In connection with the consideration of this Bill, I took the trouble to communicate with an American banker in New York and with several others witlh reference to their experience in respect to this tax. This gentleman in New York said that it had given very little trouble, that it had been accepted by the community and he was entirely favourable to a tax of this kind in connection with the raising of revenue for the purposes of war.
I think that in the United States if you draw a cheque on your own bank it is not taxed, but where your cheque passes over to some other bank the stamp tax is enforced.

I would like to
draw the minister's attention to a condition of affairs in Prince Edward Island with which he is perhaps not familiar. The 76i
Department of Agriculture has, in the last few years, organized egg collecting districts and they have taken a good deal of pains to extend the system. The collectors who were appointed issued cheques in their own names. The amounts were sometimes very small. I have seen a large number of cheques given for sums below one dollar, because as the collectors went around they would collect and pay for just what eggs the farmers had. There would not be many cheques over $2. In that case what would happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Are they agents of the
Government?
I do not know. They are working under the Government system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should imagine, because the tax is so small, that they would pay it, continuing to issue cheques for small amounts, or that they might draw cheques for large amounts and pay for the eggs in currency. If they are agents of the Government, the Government will pay the tax. I do not think it will be a very considerable charge.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
That no person shall transfer a hill of exchange or promissory note to a bank in such manner as to constitute the bank the holder thereof or deliver a bill of exchange or promissory note to a bank for collection unless there is affixed thereto an adhesive stamp or unless there is impressed thereon by means of a die, a stamp of the value of two cents.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['I should imagine, because the tax is so small, that they would pay it, continuing to issue cheques for small amounts, or that they might draw cheques for large amounts and pay for the eggs in currency. If they are agents of the Government, the Government will pay the tax. I do not think it will be a very considerable charge.']

Does that extend to every
cheque on every bank, or only to cheques on chartered banks? Is the word " bank " defined?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The word " bank " will
be defined in the Bill which I shall present after these resolutions have been adopted, so as to cover all institutions or individuals carrying on the business of banking or accepting deposits. For instance, loan companies, trust companies and other institutions and firms and individuals holding deposits subject to cheques. Otherwise, of course, the tax would be most unfair to the banks. In the Bill, we are giving the word " bank " a very wide interpretation.
Does the minister intend to include the agricultural banks of Quebec organized under provincial charters ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They cannot carry on a banking business if they are organized under provincial charters.
They receive deposits from their own members. I suppose they issue cheques of some kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they take money on deposits and give receipts, they will have to pay.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend consulted the Department of Justice with regard to this section ? It says:
That no person shall transfer a hill of exchange or promissory note to a bank-
I think it would be more accurate to say:
That no bank shall receive a bill of exchange or promissory note.
I suppose if a note is brought to a bank, the bank will not receive it unless it is properly stamped ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the Bill there will be a prohibition against a bank paying a bill of exchange or promissory note unless it is properly stamped.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wording in section 9, to which my hon. friend has drawn attention, has precedents in the Bills of Exchange Act.
Can the minister explain the difference between the use of the adhesive stamp and of the die stamp ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Either can be used. The adhesive stamp will be an Inland Revenue stamp which may be bought and placed upon the cheque, bill of exchange or note by the individual issuing it. In England, embossed cheques are issued under regulations of the Inland Revenue Department, so that the individual has not to impress the stamp. As to whether the banks here will use embossed cheques or not, I am not prepared to say at the moment. Railway companies and other large institutions *may adopt that method so as to save the trouble of putting on the stamps.
If a man issues a cheque and does not put a two cent stamp on it, what is the penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A penalty of $50 on an individual and $100 on a bank. It is only a penalty. We have been careful so that the legality of a transaction shall not be impeached by our legislation.

In case a man issues a cheque and forgets to put a two cent stamp on it, can a bank put on a stamp and charge it to the depositor?
IMr. W. T. White.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The issuer of the cheque would be liable; but if he forgot to put on the stamp, the bank would call his attention to it, and either supply him with a stamp or charge it to him.

Presumably the mechanism of English banks would be followed. There is nothing that strikes one coming from Great Britain to Canada more than the careless and slovenly way in which cheques lie all over bank counters. In England a cheque is a very sacred document. Direct taxation always tends to carefulness and accuracy, and to an improvement in the character of the people. In England a man gets about thirty cheques at a time in a book, and the cost is put on the debit side of his account in the book. The cheque book of a private citizen in Great Britain is a very sacred book, as sacred as Scripture.
Will the stamps be sold by the postmasters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Provision is being made for their being sold by postmasters and inland revenue officers and other persons, by regulations to be established by the Inland Revenue Department.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
That no person shall sign a receipt for money paid to him by a bank chargeable against a deposit of money in the bank to his credit until he has affixed to the receipt an adhesive stamp, or unless there is impressed thereon by means of a die, a stamp of the value of two cents.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Provision is being made for their being sold by postmasters and inland revenue officers and other persons, by regulations to be established by the Inland Revenue Department.']
Will that apply to the post office savings bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is money paid by a bank, not by a post office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason that provision was inserted will be obvious to my right hon. friend. If there were a stamp upon a cheque and no stamp upon a receipt, the money would be withdrawn by the latter system.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is all right, I am not objecting.
Would that embrace the signing by a bank teller of a duplicate deposit receipt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not cover that case. That is only a matter connected with the book-keeping of a bank.

The minister has in view that money deposited in the savings de-

partment of a bank is taken out more bireceipts than by cheques.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
12. That every bank having in possesssion in Canada, any promissory note, cheque or other bill of exchange made or drawn out of Canada on which a stamp has not been affixed or impressed shall, before payment or presentment for payment, if the same is payable in Canada, affix thereto an adhesive stamp of the value of two cents and the value of the stamp so affixed shall be payable to the bank by the person entitled to the proceeds of the note, cheque or bill.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['The minister has in view that money deposited in the savings de-\n\npartment of a bank is taken out more bireceipts than by cheques.']

Many American firms deposit in Canadian banks, and in paying on this side send cheques on those banks. Will this tax of two cents have to be paid on cheques drawn in the United States upon Canadian banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
14. That no money order or postal note shall be issued under the provisions of the Post Office Act until there Is affixed thereto a postage stamp of the value of two cents and one cent respectively to be paid for by the purchaser of the order or postal note, and upon such stamp there may be. printed or impressed the words "war tax".

speakerposition: subtopic
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has my hon. friend no pangs of conscience here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I had no more trouble
with my conscience than is given me by hon. gentlemen opposite I should be a happy man. Surely the right hon. gentleman does not think I am troubled in conscience over bringing down so commendable a measure as this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is the
reason I asked the question. It seems I paid the hon. gentleman an undeserved compliment in supposing that his conscience would trouble him. He is going to increase the postage by one cent. Why not have one stamp only instead of two?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section applies to
postal notes and money orders and not to letters and post-cards-these come under the next section.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The general
principle applies here also that I was pointing out that this will be a great annoyance to business. Taking this in connection with the next section, why have two stamps instead of one? One will accomplish the object as well as two, one of them stamped "war tax".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The mill will provide that an ordinary postage-stamp may be used. That will have to be covered by regulations
of the post office. We will make a minimum of inconvenience for business in the collection of this tax, just as in the case of the collection of the tax on letters. If the party sending the letter or post-card will put on the ordinary postage-stamp, it would be accepted even though it is not designated " war tax."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am glad of that. I thought it was obligatory to put on a special war tax stamp.

Does the hon. minister
intend to recognize the fact that there are two official languages in this country in the making of these war tax stamps? Especially seeing that the war is being carried on by the Allies, it would be well-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do not have it in French; it is bad enough in English.
I second the suggestion of my hon. friend from Bonaven-turo (Mr. Marcil).

I have not yet had an
answer from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would point out to my
hon. friend that these stamps will be issued by the Department of Inland Revenue. To tell the truth, I have not turned my mind upon the question of their form or character, but have simply brought down the measure in which the stamp tax is provided for. But instead of the " war tax " stamp to be devised and issued by the Inland Revenue Department, an ordinary one cent postage-stamp may be used. I suppose my hon. friend knows-I do not know because I have not inquired into it-what the regulations of the department are with respect to the one cent postage-stamp.

There are people in Quebec who are not familiar with the English language. No member of this House knows that better than does the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue who was very sympathetic at one time to the use of the French language. The former Postmaster General, Mr. Pelletier, put three French words on our post-cards, and at once we had protests from certain quarters and one would have thought that that gentleman had committed a great crime. The Minister of Finance knows that the official language of the International Postal Union is French. Therefore, the former Postmaster General was only trying to follow up what is done among the nations of the earth generally. If there is to be an inscription on these new stamps

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: it should be in a language the people will understand.

I strongly support
the idea that this inscription should be in French as well as in English. I think your electors, Mr. Chairman, (Mr. Sevigny) and those of the Minister of Inland Revenue <Mr. Blondin) like others, are entitled to know that they will pay that tax on account of the participation of Canada in the war of the Empire.

In order to do away with any trouble which might arise with the use of English or French, I would make the suggestion that we should come back to the original language, that spoken in the Garden of Eden-Gaelic, and that these Stamps should be inscribed in that language.

Postal notes are used for amounts as low as 20 cents. Does the minister not think there should be no taxation upon postal notes for less than 25 cents ? Upon a 20-cent or 25-cent postal note the taxation proposed would be very heavy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will average up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
15. That on every letter and post-card for transmission by post a tax of one cent shall he levied and collected, such tax to be payable by affixing to the letter or card a postage-stamp of that denomination, upon which there may be printed or impressed the words " war tax " ;

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why not have only one stamp instead of two stamps, and so provide P

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that it is not advisable to appear to be amending the Post Office Act. One might as well say: Why not raise your postage to 2 cents and 3 cents ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Although my Tight hon. friend says " hear, hear," I am sure he would not consider that to be advisable. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We know that this is for war; we all hope that it is only temporary, as I believe it will be. At all events, for the time that it is in existence, why submit the public to the necessity of licking two stamps instead of one ? It is quite sufficient to say that it is an unpleasant operation, especially to those who send letters by the hundreds every day. Why not have a 3-cent stamp r Everybody will understand that it is for war purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not believe there will be much inconvenience. My hon. friend speaks of licking the stamps, but if hundreds of letters a day are sent by a firm, the stamps are not licked; they have other means of meeting the situation. However, I shall be glad to take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration.

If a letter is posted having an ordinary 2-cent stamp and an ordinary 1

cent stamp upon it, will it go just the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It goes whether or not the 1-cent stamp is marked " war tax." My hon. friend will observe that the provision is permissive; it says that the words "war tax" may be impressed upon the stamp.
Can the Minister of Finance assure the committee that all the revenue arising from this extra taxation will be applied to war purposes, and will not go into the ordinary revenue of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that all the moneys of the Dominion go into one fund; they are mingled. The reason why we are calling this a war tax is this: the country is at war; revenues are diminished, and we are required to find money to meet, in addition to the ordinary expenditure required to carry on the affairs of the country, the interest upon the debt which we shall incur in borrowing for the purposes of our participation in the war. In addition to that there will be pension charges upon the Government. But, putting this all aside,
I desire to say now, without the slightest intention of stirring up any discussion in the matter, that even if not a dollar of the money would go for the specific purposes of the war-that is to say, be ear-marked and specifically applied to some purpose immediately connected with the war-the tax would still be purely a war tax, because the only reason for its imposition is

that the country is at war and that the normal revenues are not sufficient to meet the abnormal strain which is upon us. Many of the arguments put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite are weighty, but I must say that I have not been in the least impressed with the force of the argument that these taxes are not war taxes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Neither have
we upon this side of the House been impressed with the argument that these taxes are war taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let it go at that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Very well.
Whether this is a war tax or whether it is not a war tax, it will all- go into one fund; there is no necessity of ear-marking it as a war tax. This method of imposing the additional stamp tax is simply causing new inconvenience to the community, and I think my hon. friend, upon reflection, will agree that he had better drop the idea.

It is going to be a great inconvenience to the people of this country to have to affix two stamps to their letters and post-cards. I cannot for the life of me see why a 3-cent stamp cannot be issued, particularly in view of the fact, as the minister says, that the war tax is not separate from the ordinary revenue of the country. I think that if a 3-cent stamp were issued the business and mercantile community would be saved a great deal of inconvenience.
I understand the minister to say that the use of the war stamp is not compulsory; that an ordinary stamp will answer the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Taking all these items one by one, how much revenue does the minister expect to obtain from the article perfumery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Does the minister think there is as much perfumery used as patent medicines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The word perfumery is given a wide definition in the Act so as to cover cosmetics and a considerable range of articles.
Is it possible to define what is meant by proprietary medicines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think so. The definition is as follows:
" Proprietary or patent medicine " includes pills, powders, tinctures, troches, or lozenges, syrups, cordials, bitters, anodynes, tonics, plasters, liniments, salves, ointments, pastes, drops, waters (except mineral waters in their natural state or carbonized), essences, oils, and all other medicinal preparations or compositions bottled or packed ready for sale in respect of which the person making or preparing the same has or claims to have any formula or secret oi occult art for the making or preparing thereof, or has or claims to have any exclusive right or title to such making or preparing, or which are prepared or made under any letters patent or which are designated by a trade mark or which if prepared in accordance with any formula published or unpublished are recommended to the public by the makers, vendors, or proprietors thereof as remedies or specifics for any disease or affection whatsoever affecting the human or animal body, but does not include any medicinal preparation or composition recognized by the British or the United States pharmacopoeia or the French codex as officinal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the meaning of that word "officinal"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I asked that question to-day, but I have forgotten the definition. My deputy, however, assures me it is a good word.
Might I ask where that definition comes from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It comes partly from our own tariff, partly from the United States, and part of it has been adapted to meet the situation. But the essential feature of the proprietary medicine is that it does not include any medicine, preparation or composition recognized by the British or the United States pharmacopoeia or the French Codex as officinal.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With respect to the pharmacopoeia preparations, there is no exclusive right, there is no privilege, and there are no letters patent. The pharmacopoeia preparations are made up from the formulae of the pharmocopoeia, and the tax would not apply to them.

I am not very clear on the point, and I think it is important to have it clear. We talk about proprietary medicines. I understood the minister to say it is only when such a medicine is sold in packages by the druggist, in six or eight ounce bottles for instance, that the tax is imposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the consumer.

To-day what are called proprietary medicines are used very extensively in doctors' prescriptions. The Parke Davis firm sell to the druggist a Winchester bottle which would contain as much as a great many six ounce or eight ounce bottles. As I understand, the tax does not apply to doctors' prescriptions. It must be in packages, such as four, six or twelve ounces, as sold by the druggist?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, sold to the consumer.
If it is sold by a druggist to a company doctor, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
