My hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) is addressing himself to the question of proprietary medicines only. Consumer is defined as follows:
Consumer means a person who uses up a proprietary or patent medicine. . . . either in serving his own wants or in producing therefrom any article of value, and " selling to a consumer," includes selling by retail.
So that if the article were purchased and used in the making of a compound and then

sold, the party so using it would be a consumer.

I am not quite clear on that point yet. Wampole's cod liver oil, which is probably known to every member in the House, goes to the druggist in a large bottle called a " Winchester ". Now suppose a doctor prescribes ten ounces of Wampole's cod liver oil, does the consumer pay the tax on that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The tax is paid
on the bottle:

If the druggist divided the winchester of cod liver oil into two six-ounce bottles, I could understand that the consumer would pay the two or five cents, whatever it may be; but when a man takes a doctor's prescription for ten ounces of cod liver oil to the druggist, has he to pay the stamp tax when the druggist hands him the cod liver oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may or may not be; you cannot pronounce on that until you know the facts. But if it were a proprietary medicine, then, under this definition, the doctor or druggist would be a consumer, for he would be using the cod liver oil to produce therefrom another article of value; that is, he would use it in making up a prescription.
My hon. friend from Souris does not mean it as a mixture. Suppose it was not compounded with anything else?

I say that on the
ordinary druggist's shelf to-day there are twenty-five or more different winchesters, one containing Wampole's cod liver oil, another Wyeth's Mixture, another Lyman and Jones' Mixture, and so on. I should say that fifty to seventy-five per cent of the business done by druggists to-day is done in that way. When I prescribe a six-ounce bottle of Wampole's Cod Liver Oil or any other preparation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend uses the
word " or " ?
-or any other preparation that goes to the druggist in a winchester, would that come under the stamp tax? In my opinion it would not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is a proprietary medicine I should say that it would, for the reason that the definition says:
Every person selling to a consumer any bottle or package containing a proprietary or patent medicine
and so on. The size of the bottle is not defined, and even if the proprietary medicine was broken up from larger bulk, I should say that the tax would apply.
Then it would apply to 75 per cent of all that is sold by the ordinary druggist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, if it is a proprietary medicine.

On section 17-proprietary or patent
medicines, etc.:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing the question of proprietary medicines, and with the view of giving the committee an explanation of what will come within the definition, I desire to make the following statement: Proprietary medicines are only such medicines as are recommended to the public by the makers, vendors, or proprietors thereof as remedies or specifics for any disease or affection whatsoever affecting the human or animal body.
Medicines prepared by druggists from several drugs or ingredients in accordance with physicians' prescriptions are not proprietary medicines.
Proprietary medicines purchased by drug-prietary medicine have already paid the purpose of being re-packed in smaller packages, without the addition of any drug or ingredient, for sale to individuals, become liable to stamp tax at the time of sale by the druggists.
Would not the proprietary medicine have already paid the tax ? Is it to be paid a second time when the druggist divides it up and sells it ? It would pay the tax twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Proprietary medicines purchased by druggists in bulk and large

packages, for the purpose of being repacked in smaller packages, without the addition of any drug or ingredient, for sale to individuals, become liable to stamp tax at the time of sale by the druggists.
They would have to pay the tax twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Would the tax not be paid on this medicine when it was bought ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not until they break up the package and sell it. The stamp will bo placed on the article at the time of sale for reasons that I shall explain a little later. Proprietary medicines purchased by druggists and used by them for compounding with other drugs or ingredients in accordance with physicians' prescriptions, must have the stamp affixed to the bottle or container before being opened by the druggist, as he is* the consumer, the compounded article not being a proprietary medicine. In answer to my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), if what is-clearly a patent medicine is used in the compounding of a mixture, which is sold to the public, it is perfectly clear that the mixture or compound is not a patent medicine. If, in connection with a prescription which is filled, taking a six-ounce bottle, two ounces of compound, or proprietary, medicine is used with other drugs and ingredients to the extent of four ounces, making a bottle of six ounces, it is obvious that the resultant mixture is not a patent or proprietary medicine, but a medicine compounded from a prescription and consequently differing from any one of the ingredients, including the patent or proprietary medicine used in connection with it. To give an illustration: Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen; that is what is covered by the formula H2O. You have water which is different from either oxygen or hydrogen, or different from either of its constituents.	>
What is that word you were going'to give us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I knew that my hon. friend would be interested in that word. I know how interested my hon. friend is in the precise meaning of terms. I have gone to the trouble-no, I have given myself the pleasure-of having this looked up for my hon. friend's benefit. I know that he is a purist in the use of English, and is interested in all definitions. " Officinal "- facio, I think, would be the Latin root 
word-opus and facio-doing work, performing, accomplishing things, just as this Government has been doing; you might almost describe it as an officinal Government.
That is the wrong word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) would say so, but we will not go into that now.
Officinal : 1. Applied in pharmacy to preparations made according to recognized prescriptions ; specifically, prescribed in the pharmacopoeia.
2. Specifically, a drug prepared according to
the pharmacopoeia.
Derivation:	Latin, officina - a workshop,
laboratory-probably a combination of opus and facio. Officina is a contraction for opiflcina.
I think this is an illuminating definition for my hon. friend. This definition has been considered very carefully by representatives of the wholesale, manufacturing and retail druggists, and I think it can be depended upon as meeting the situation.
What is the definition of " perfumery?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perfumery includes alcoholic and non-alcoholic perfumes, and perfumed spirits, bay rum, cologne, lavender waters, hair-oil, tooth and other powders, and washes, pomatums, pastes, and all other preparations used for hair, mouth and skin.
Does that include talcum powder?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tooth and other powders. Yes.

I notice that the minister has made the stamp tax one cent for any bottle or package of the value of 25 cents or less, and
More than twenty-five cents-
For each twenty-five cents and in addition for any fractional part of twenty-five cents	One cent.
That means an increase of 4 per cent. I do not know what it should be. Before recess, the minister said that his conscience was quite clear on some items. A man travelling on a train has to pay 5 per cent on his railway fare, and a man who can afford to buy perfume ought to pay more than 4 per cent. This luxury should be taxed a little higher. My sympathy is with the ladies of this country, but we are here to do business in a proper manner. I hope the minister will see his way clear to let

go this 5 per cent on railway fares for amounts around one dollar, and increase the duty on perfume.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax is a pretty heavy one. My hon. friend will observe that the tax is upon 25 cents or less. One cent upon 5 cents would be 20 per cent; one cent upon 10 cents would be 10 per cent; one cent upon 20 cents would be 5 per cent; one cent upon 25 cents, it is true, would be 4 per cent. Another consideration should be borne in mind, namely, that this is, so to speak, a domestic tax. There is a duty upon these articles coming in as well. Therefore the tax that we are imposing will be sufficiently heavy, especially as it is in addition to the taxation resulting from the import duty upon those articles. The tax of 10 per cent, which we had originally, was really too high, especially when added to the import duty. After giving the matter exceedingly careful consideration and after consulting with all the interests concerned, we came to the conclusion that the tax might be modified and that the resolution should be changed to its present form.

The druggists handling these articles were hard hit in August when the tax was made pretty high on alcohol, which a great many of those articles contain. I am pleased that the Minister of Finance has considered that matter, and that he has relieved the druggists, because as this resolution was worded originally as regards perfumery, the druggists were harder hit than were any other class for whom we are legislating.
Is the definition of perfumerv which the minister gave us to be the statutory definition5

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What about
the tax on champagne? I ask this question having regard to the French treaty. Can we impose the duty on account of the French treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there were any doubt
on the subject, I should not have brought down the proposal. In the opinion of the Department of Justice it is perfectly clear that we have the power to levy this, which is an excise tax, not a customs tax. I draw the attention of my right hon. friend to article 12 of the French treaty which my right hon. friend has before h:m. The convention is of 1907, although the treaty did not
come into operation until a couple of years later. Article 12 reads:
Products of Canadian origin of any kind imported into France, Algeria, the French colonies and possessions and the territories of the protectorate of Indo-China, shall not be subject to any higher or other duties of excise, internal consumption or octroi-
Which is a city tax, I believe.
-than those which are or may be charged upon products of French origin.
In like manner, products of any kind originating in France, Algeria, the French colonies and possessions and the territories of the protectorate of Indo-China, shall not be subject to any higher or other duties of excise, internal consumption, or octroi than those which are or may be charged on like products of Canadian origin.
This tax that we are imposing is a general tax not only upon goods imported from France, but upon goods produced in Canada and in other countries. Therefore so far as the imposition of this excise duty is concerned there is no discrimination as regards importations from France. The French treaty provides for the admission into Canada under schedule B of a large number of items, including spirits, alcoholic perfumes, medicinal or medicated wines, photographs, medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations, and a number of other articles at the intermediate rate, whatever that may be.
Under schedule C there is a long list of articles including vegetables, wines, champagnes, certain books and certain medicinal, chemical and pharmaceutical preparations, olive oil, embroideries, velvets, ribbons and manufacture of silk, which are to be admitted at a fixed and specific rate of duty which it is not open to this Government, without violation of the treaty, to increase. Those are duties of customs, as is so expressed in the convention. I had regard for that in the proposal brought down. I was unable to raise the duty, as I think I otherwise would have been disposed to do, upon a number of articles of luxury embraced in this schedule C of the French treaty, because of the fact that those articles are entitled to the benefits of that schedule 0 when imported from France. Therefore we did not increase the duty. With regard to wines, which I think every one will admit are a proper subject for taxation at a time like this, we have been advised by the Department of Justice-and I think it is perfectly obvious on a reading of the treaty-that it is open to the Government to impose a stamp tax, which is in the nature of an excise duty, upon wines,

non-sparkling and upon sparkling wines and champagne. I think there is nothing we have done in any way inconsistent with the express terms of the French treaty, nor anything in which it is not open to the French Governmeent, should it so desire, to take similar action.

Why does the minister discriminate so heavily between sparkling and non-sparkling wines? There are nonsparkling wines that are quite as expensive as the sparkling wines. The difference in the tax is so great that I should like to understand the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I were to answer with levity, I suppose I should say that it is because we want the people to pay something for the sparkle. But, speaking seriously, the non-sparkling wine is generally cheaper than the sparkling wine or champagne. That classification is made, I think, in the French treaty; at all events it is made in the tariff, and we are following precedent in making that classification here. Champagne, of course, is an exceedingly expensive wine, much too expensive, I suppose, for my hon. friend, as it is for me.
Non-sparkling wine is sometimes more expensive than sparkling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I defer to my hon. friend's opinion, if he is more an expert than I, though he may not be.

The minister has not explained why, on articles included in the French Convention, he imposes no additional tax, even when they come from another country-I refer to luxuries such as silks and velvets. My hon. friend knows that a great many of these articles that are included in the French Convention are brought also from the United States. Why should they not be taxed when coming from countries other than France? That is one question I should like to ask the minister. The other is this: I would like him to take us into his confidence and tell us the reasons which influenced him in the amendments which he has made in this resolution in order to make it legal and not in contravention of the French treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand.
I say the minister should take us into his confidence and let us know why the changes were made in order to make it not contrary to the French Convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon, gentleman mean, since I brought it dowrU
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No changes were made to my knowledge for that purpose. I can assure my hon. friend that my assistant deputy has had the drafting of this Bill, and I think he has done it very competently. To my knowledge no changes were made for the purpose of bringing these proposals into conformity with the French treaty. It was quite unnecessary, in my view, to consider such a question. I looked carefully into the matter, and we were specifically advised in connection with the proposals which we laid before the House, that this tax being an excise tax, our action was not in the least in violation of the express provision of the French Convention.

The assistant deputy
minister deserves the greatest possible credit. He has shown great ability, and when he gives attention to changes of this kind he would certainly make all necessary provision. But if he has not given thought to the subject his instinct is remarkable-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unerring.

-for he has taken out of the resolution the very words to which I objected when I addressed the House and the removal of which bring the resolution into conformity with the French Convention. Let me read what was in the resolution and what has been left out of the amended resolution which is now before the committee. At page 99 of unrevised Hansard* the hon. gentleman will find section 15 of the resolution as it was read to the House by the Minister of Finance, as follows:
15. That the provisions of any Act founded or. these resolutions, in so far as such provisions relate to wine, non-sparkling, champagne and sparkling wine, shall he deemed to have come into force on the twelfth day of February, 1915, and to have applied to all such articles

(a) imported or taken out of customs warehouse for consumption on and after that day and to have also applied to such articles previously imported for which no customs entry was made before that day.
The words " imported or taken out of customs warehouse for consumption on or after that day, etc.," have been entirely omitted from the present amended resolution, and it is made simply a stamp tax to be paid by a stamp placed upon the article by the person selling to the consumer the bottle or package of wine. That puts the case in a different position entirely. What I challenged when addressing the House was this provision that before imported goods could be taken out of the customs

warehouse an additional tax should be paid whether by way of stamp or any other way. Now, somebody, with wisdom and, as I say with most remarkable instinct, has left out all these words and made this simply an internal stamp tax to be affixed to the bottle when the vendor sells it, and not when it is taken out of customs. Does not the hon. gentleman see the difference? And is not he proud of the instinct which enabled such a change to be made in a resolution as to get'rid of the difficulty which I pointed out, the words being in contravention of the provisions of the French treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The taking out of the clause to which my hon. friend has referred, had no connection whatever with his argument or with the idea which was at the foundation of that argument. The reason why it was taken out-

I thought the minister
said there were no changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No changes having any
bearing upon the question whether or not this was in contravention of the French treaty. There is a very simple explanation. It was pointed out both by the Customs Department and by the importers of these wines that to open up all the boxes and packages and put a stamp upon each bottle while in the custody of the Customs Department would give an enormous amount of trouble and inconvenience. The result is that the stamps are now to be affixed at the time of sale to the consumer. The object Tyas not to meet any difficulties in connection with the French treaty, but to meet a practical objection on the part of the Customs Department and of those engaged in the importation of wines. My hon. friend will see that this is a pure, synchronism. My hon. friend is a good lawyer when he is impartially advising a client, but not when he is addressing the House of Commons; consequently he will forgive me if I do not attach the weight to Shis opinion that I would if it were given in a case in which he had no object in exercising any political bias. I need not insult the intelligence of the House by saying that there is a clear distinction between duties of customs and duties of excise. The French treaty is a document to be interpreted according to the well-known rules of legal construction, and personally I should be against a strained construction. There is no room for doubt that if the duties are not increased it is open to this Government to enact that excise duties
by way of stamp taxation may be imposed upon those goods once they arrive in Canada, whether they are in the custody of the Customs Department-which is only an incident-or not, provided that Canadian goods of a similar character are treated in identically the same manner. Therefore my hon. friend's legal opinion was unsound. The change was made for the purpose that I have indicated, and for no other. However, as the result makes my hon. friend the member for St. John happy, of course we are all happy, for I need not say that it is our object so to conduct thebusiness of the country as to meet the approval not only of the public, but of gentlemen on both sides of this House. I understand, then, that any objection my hon. friend had to the imposition of these stamp duties in the case of wines, non-sparkling and sparkling, and champagne, is withdrawn, because a legal difficulty which he thought he saw is now non-existent.
The sad part of it is that when the hon. gentleman gropes his way blindly he seems to go more unerringly than when he proceeds with his eyes open.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I always had a good opinion of the Civil Service, and I always tell the officers of my department to keep a pretty good check on me and to criticise me severely. My hon. friend has paid a tribute to my assistant deputy. Allow me to say that I join very gladly in that tribute, because he has done his work in a manner that will commend itself, I think, to the members of the House.
My hon. friend has referred to another matter. He says: Why did you not raise the duties upon these articles coming in from other countries? We had a tariff in which, under the French convention, the goods in question were subject to a specific duty which could not be increased. The tariff upon goods coming in from other countries had been fixed. I know that the Government is not obligated to do it, but in considering tariff matters, regard must be had, in a sense, to the family of nations, and if you take an action which seems invidious or unjust or unduly discriminatory against other nations, you are apt to raise questions which may lead to retaliation. I understand that some years ago- I speak from recollection, I believe it was in connection with this very treaty-some question was raised as between the United States and Canada with regard to what was alleged to be discriminatory treatment. That matter was adjusted by some con-
12n

cessions. Having regard to the whole situation, it occurred to us that it would be inexpedient and inadvisable that we should deliberately raise the duties upon this class of articles in respect of which the duties under the French convention were fixed and specific, unless some consideration of paramount importance inclined us to do so. The fact of the matter is that our minds were not turned particularly upon the subject at all. It seems to me to be rather invidious ana aiscriminatory treatment to raise the tariff on goods coming from all other countries.
Mr. MARCH.:	Are French wines given
any preference over German wines, or are they on the same footing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The French treaty is the basis of all most favoured nation treatment in the way of fiscal legislation so far as this country is concerned. The French treaty goes farthest. Under it certain articles are entitled to the benefits of the intermediate tariff. Then there is schedule C, a most important schedule, in which the rates of duties upon a number of commodities which I have mentioned, such as velvet and silks, alcoholic perfumes, wines-non-sparkling- champagne and a number of other commodities, are specific. Only those nations which are entitled to the most favoured nation treatment are entitled also to the benefits of the provisions of the French treaty, which, as I say, is the most favourable treaty that any foreign nation has with us. Germany has not been entitled to most favoured nation treatment from Canada. The matter had on many occasions been submitted to the Government, but we had not been able to see our way to accord to Germany a most favoured nation treatment which would put her on a par with other nations in respect of the provisions of the French Convention of 1907, which, as I say, came into effect in 1909. Germany, therefore, was not, previous to the outbreak of the war-and, of course, is not to-day- entitled to the benefits of the French treaty.
What I want to know is whether wines which are in the country and which have come from France are subject to the same treatment as those which have come from Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to wines which are in the country at the present time, whether Canadian, French or German, upon sale the taxation would apply, because our object is to raise money for the object of fighting Germany
So far as these new excise duties are concerned, are French and German wines on the same footing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think French and German wines are not on the same basis, for this reason: French wines that are in the country now have already derived the benefit of the French treaty; German wines now in this country did not derive the benefit of that treaty, because Germany did not have that advantage. These wines, being in the country are owned by Canadians. This measure is an excise measure, as I have stated, for the purpose of raising a revenue upon the sales of wines to consumers, whether those wines be Canadian, British, French, German or otherwise.

If the minister insists
that the stamp tax shall be imposed only when the wine is sold by the importer to a customer, he is opening very wide the door for men who use wine in considerable quantities to do their own importing, thus avoiding the payment of the stamp tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why?
Because if they import the wines themselves, they can take them out of bond and if they use the wine themselves and do not sell it they do not have to put on any stamps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is covered by the Bill -in such a case the importer is a consumer: In the case of an importer bringing in wine for his own use the stamp would have to be paid.
But suppose he does not choose to put the stamp on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He cannot get it through the customs until the stamp is on.
But the minister says the stamp does not go on until after the wine has passed the customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That will be covered by the Bill. It will be dealt with in this way. The Customs Department will determine whether the man who imports is a wholesaler or a consumer. They have an efficient organization and they can do that. A wholesaler bringing in goods may be permitted, without breaking bulk and having the stamp tax imposed while the goods are in bond, to take them out under regulations of the Customs Department, under which the tax will be paid before the wine is sold to consumers. My hon. friend has pointed out a possible loop-hole, but the Customs will see

that the loop-hole is closed under regulations that will be established.
I presumed the Bill would be founded on the resolutions and there is no such provision in them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many matters of detail that are set out in the Bill that are not included in the resolutions, which are necessarily general in character.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I may say that my hon. friend has satisfied me that he has power under the French Treaty to put this tax upon all wines except champagne. Upon every other wine, for instance those mentioned in the first article of section 0, wine of the grape, non-sparkling, under the French Treaty he can impose a tax; but with regard to champagne or sparkling wine, the provision of the French Treaty, the general governing clause, is in these words:
There shall be levied, collected and paid for the said convention if brought into force, and so long as it remains in force, upon all natural and manufactured products enumerated in schedule B to the said convention, originating in France, Algeria, the French colonies and possessions, and the territories of the protectorate of Indo-China, imported into Canada in the manner provided in the said convention, the several rates of duties of customs set forth in column 2, " intermediate tariff," of the customs tariff, 1907, and in any amendment thereof; and there shall be levied, collected and paid, during the time aforesaid, upon all natural and manufactured products enumerated in schedule C to the said convention, originating and imported as aforesaid, the several rates of duties of customs set opposite to each item respectively in the said schedule C.
My hon. friend says, however, that this is a special tax and we have the power to . impose a special tax under article 12. Article 12 of the French Convention is:
In like manner, products of any kind originating in France, Algeria, the French colonies and possessions, and the territories of the protectorate of Indo-China, when imported into Canada shall not be subject to any other or higher duties of excise, internal consumption or octroi than those which are or may be charged upon like products of Canadian origin.
Under these resolutions a special tax is levied and, as has been stated by the minister to the hon. member for Bon-aventure (Mr. Marcil) the tax applies to wines whether from France, Germany, the United States or any other country in the world. The moment they come into consumption they are subject to the tax, and it is obvious that the French, who were looking after their own interests, provided in this way: While the customs tax shall
not be more than it is at present. $3.30 a gallon, if you impose a tax upon other wines which come in competition with your own you shall have the same privilege of putting the duty on our wines as you put upon your own. That, I understand, is the principle. The point which I make is that champagne is a French wine the like of which is not produced in any other country. There are sparkling wines manufactured in other countries, in Germany for instance, but the special wine which is called champagne is produced in France and in France alone. Therefore, this article 12 cannot apply to champagne although it may be applied to other wines. The Treaty could not foresee that there would be imposed any excise duty on any other similar wine, because there is no similar wine produced anywhere else. It therefore seems to me that under the Treaty you cannot apply section 12 to champagne. The French Commissioners, when negotiating with our Commissioners, must have foreseen that their still wines would come in competition with other wines and that upon those wines there would be excise duty. When we passed the Treaty in 1907 we had wine produced in Canada with which the French wine would come in competition. The French Commissioners foresaw that there would be an excise duty put upon our own wines, and that the French wines would be subject to the same excise duty. But they could not foresee that their champagne would come in competition with any other wine because there are no similar wines produced in the world. This is a Treaty which ought to be construed liberally. The great wealth of France-and France is a very rich country-comes from her vintages. The wine crop of France is her greatest asset, and the French are naturally desirous of extending their trade all over the world, and they have done so. They have a right to a liberal construction of their Treaty, and when they provided that their champagne should be exempted from any special tax they had the right to expect that the Treaty would ' be generously applied, especially under such circumstances as exist to-day. v
As I have said, champagne is produced in no country except France. At first I should have been disposed to believe that-this tax would not apply to all French wines, but it seems that it does; I wish my hon. friend would take this view into-his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I might point out that
under article 12 it is provided that:

Products of any kind originating in France, Algeria, the French colonies and possessions, and the territories of the protectorate of IndoChina, when imported into Canada shall not be subject to any other or higher duties of excise, internal consumption or octroi than those which are or may be charged upon like products of Canadian origin.
Upon a purely legal construction of Article 12, there is no doubt in my mind that, if the Canadian Government does not impose upon Canadian products a lower duty than is imposed upon French products coming into Canada, we shall be strictly observing the requirements of this French Convention. My right hon. friend makes this point. He says that as a matter of fact champagne is not produced in Canada and therefore it is not possible for us, even if we desire to do so, to impose upon a like product of Canadian origin the duty that we now propose to put upon champagne. Now the word " like " is a word that is not on all fours with the word " identical," and it appears clear to me that, even if by chance a like product should be produced in Canada at any time or is being produced even now, it is open to the Government to impose this tax; and I think that upon a strictly legal interpretation of Article 12 it would be so held by any court. That is my own opinion. My right hon. friend holds a different opinion, and undoubtedly his opinion is entitled to great weight. I had said before my hon. friend mentioned it that my disposition would be to interpret this treaty not in any strained fashion; I think those are the words I used. Everybody in this House will admit that if any tax for war purposes is justified at the present time, it is this tax upon wines, and especially upon champagne, because those who can afford to purchase champagne can probably afford better than any other class in the community to contribute to the expenses of this war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore in principle our legislation is absolutely sound, and the only question that remains is:
9	p.m. Does our proposed action in any way conflict with or violate the express and literal terms of the French Convention, or is it in substantial violation of that convention, giving it a liberal instead of a strained and unduly narrow legal interpretation?' So far as the suggestion of my right hon. friend is concerned, I shall go this far. The Bills founded upon these resolutions will be introduced to-night. I shall draw his remarks to the attention of

the Department of Justice, and if it is found that there is room for doubt whether we are violating the provisions of the French Convention of 1907, I shall be very glad to bring the matter before the Government with the view of seeing whether our proposals should be in any degree modified.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The statement of my hon. friend is quite satisfactory. I
could not ask for more. I agree altogether with him that if there is any class of articles which ought to be taxed it is articles of luxury, and there is no greater luxury than champagne. As far as that goes I am absolutely at one with my hon. friend. The only thing I wish to draw his attention to is this. It is essential that we should keep good faith in our treaties. We are at war to-day because a treaty has not been observed. We should observe this treaty, not only in the letter, but in the spirit also; and if there is anything in my contention, and I believe there is, this treaty ought to be generously interpreted. Let me remind my hon. friend of what took place after the adoption of the Washington treaty which made fish free in the United States. There was what we thought to be a violation of the treaty, and we made representations to Washington, but our representations were of no avail, and from that day to this we have always been under the impression that the United States had in fact violated the spirit if not the letter of the treaty. I am quite agreeably impressed with the statement made by my hon. friend that he will refer the matter to the Department of Justice. The only thing I would add is that if there is any doubt at all it should be given in favour of the treaty.

I wish to say a word with regard to the articles of luxury contained in Schedule C of the French treaty. I cannot agree with the reasons given by my hon. friend for exempting some of these articles when coming from countries which are not entitled to the benefits given by the French Convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Italy is one.

In times like these, when these extra taxes, claimed by the Government to be war taxes, are being imposed on all the people of the country, I do not think Italy would find very much fault if an extra tax were to be put on luxuries coming from that country; nor do I think the United States would find very much fault if an extra tax were placed upon silks, velvets, and embroideries coming from the United States into Canada. I

am not at all able to agree with my hon. friend. What are the articles exempted so far as countries other than France are concerned, and which the minister was not bound to exempt ? Take anchovies, for instance. Anchovies come in larger quantities from Norway than they do from France, notwithstanding that France has the benefit of the French Convention. Archovies are a luxury of the rich, an appetizer which the wealthy take before dinner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
How much does my hon. friend think we should get by a tax upon anchovies ?
Mr. PUG8LEY: How much does my hon. friend expect from the one-cent stamp tax on lettere ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A great deal.

It is the aggregate that counts. We manufacture sardines in this country. Why are the sardines which come from Norway exempted from the operation of this extra tax ? Why do you exempt all fish packed in oil, whether from Norway, the United States, or any other maritime country? Do you exempt them simply because Canada has agreed to give a certain .special tariff so far as France is concerned? Take other articles.
Embroideries, n.o.p.; laces n.o.p. ; collars or collarettes in lace and all manufactures of lace; nettings of cotton; linen, silk, or other material n.o.p.	'
Velvets of pure silk and silk fabrics; ribbons of all kinds and materials ; manufactures of silk or of which silk is the component part of chief value, n.o.p.
Why are these articles exempted when they come in from other countries which are not enjoying the benefits of the French convention? If you will take the customs returns for the past year you will find that very large quantities of these articles of luxury came in from [DOT] the United States. My hon. friend recognizes that these are articles of luxury that ought not to be exempted from a general system of taxation such as is now proposed, and which is intended to be of a temporary character. But my hon. friend, knowing, as he could not help knowing, from an examination of the customs returns, that large quantities of these articles of luxury come in from the United States, knowing that these are articles used by the rich and knowing that he is taxing all articles which are worn by the masses of the people, deliberately exempts these articles coming in from other countries, and that simply because it might 77
be regarded as somewhat invidious if they were not exempted, the same as they are when coming from France. I cannot see any reason in the position taken by the Minister of Finance. A special convention was made with France. If there was any objection made by the people or Government of the United States-I dare say there would not be-Canada might very well say that under the convention with France we were not able to increase the tariff on goods coming from that country, but owing to the necessity of imposing taxes on all the people of Canada, we did not feel that we could properly exempt these articles of luxury, which are used by the rich, and therefore we imposed the same tax upon these goods that we imposed on other articles which are not articles of luxury to the same extent as these are. I cannot see any reason whatever for the action of the Government in making a total exemption in favour of the import from all countries of the world of these articles of luxury.

Mr. Chairman,
before the committee rises, I want to put myself on record as being opposed to the imposition of this taxation, which I consider unnecessary as well as vexatious, at a time when the practice of economy is so necessary by our people. I say that during the hard times which at present prevail, and with the high cost of living, it is inopportune to increase the burdens of the people. I desire, as the representative of my own division of Montreal, to place on record my opposition to a measure of this kind.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.
