speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) the House went into Committee on Bill No. 74, to amend the Criminal Code, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 2-assisting alien enemies to leave Canada:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill was reported by a special committee appointed to consider some suggestions looking to the amendment of the Criminal Code. To it were referred a Bill introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), and a Bill introduced by the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair.) Apart from that there was a suggestion made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who moved a resolution upon the subject of improvement of our laws with regard to copy-wright, looking especially to giving an additional protection to the rights of dramatic authors. There is also embodied in the Bill a provision which is the result of a suggestion coming from one of the Chief Justices of one of the High Court Divisions of Ontario, and which he deemed it proper to make in view of the result of a prosecution instituted there against a person for aiding an individual of alien enemy nationality to leave the country. In that particular case, it not being made directly to appear that the purpose of the alien enemy in leaving the country was to aid and to assist the enemy, and furthermore the mere act of aiding such a person to leave the country under those circumstances not amounting to treason, it was found that, notwithstanding the prohibition enacted against such alien enemy leaving the coun-"try, the person aiding could not be found guilty of any violation of the Criminal Code. It seemed to the learned Chief Justice, and to me, and also to the committee, desirable that provision should be made to cover such a case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was the charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The charge was that
the parties accused had aided a person of alien enemy nationality during the present war to leave the country, although it had

been deemed desirable in the Old Country- and we followed their example-to prohibit such person of alien enemy nationality from leaving the country except when, after examination by a registrar, he was granted an exeat. Therefore the person leaving the country was acting in violation of that prohibition lawfully enacted; but it was found that there was no provision in the Criminal Code which would cover the case of a person aiding and abetting him to leave the country. The parties were tried, and it was contended that such an act on the part of the accused amounted to treason; but the courts held that upon the facts as proved, the action did not amount to treason, and that there was no provision in the criminal law which would reach such a person. By this Bill, the mere aiding and abetting of a person who is of alien enemy nationality to leave the country-and we are always supposing that the name "enemy" means that we are at war with the sovereign of the nation of which the person is a subject-will be an offence how without its being necessary to establish directly on the part of the prosecution any direct purpose to aid the enemy. There are the saving words in the section, which reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who incites or assists any subject of any foreign state or country at war with His Majesty to leave Canada, if the circumstances of the case do not exclude the possibility that assistance to the enemy is an intended object in his so leaving Canada, and if such inciting or assisting do not amount to treason.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There does not seem to be very much involved. What were the particulars of that case? Were the parties charged as principals or as abettors?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not before me
the report of the case. If my memory is correct, they were charged with treason as being subjects of His Majesty taking part in an operation of a nature to be of aid or assistance to an alien enemy at war with His Majesty. While that was the idea that underlay the charge, as I understand it, the evidence did not justify the statement that the people were leaving the country with any intent to do anything in the-way of helping or assisting the enemy. So-far as the people who sought to go out were concerned, they were in the wrong in-so far as they were violating a prohibition of their going. No doubt that prohibition rested upon the assumption that in some-

way their going out might be to aid or to assist the enemy country.
They were under prohibition of going out of the country. The offence charged against the parties was that they aided or assisted them to go, and I believe the charge was made upon the assumption that such aiding or assisting would amount to treason. But the court held that it did not, and it further held that there was no provision in the criminal law making, aiding or assisting a person prohibited from going out, a criminal offence; and that the proclamation, being addressed to and applying to persons of alien enemy nationality, did not apply to the person who might assist another to disobey the prohibition of the proclamation.

It seems to me that this clause will make it a crime for a Canadian to lend money, for instance, to a man of foreign extraction to leave this country, even though he may be going to the United States. That is not a crime, and should not be made a crime by statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
omits one very essential condition. The Bill does not purport to make it a crime to assist any person of foreign nationality to leave Canada. It does make it a crime for one to assist a person of alien enemy nationality whose country is at war with His Majesty to leave Canada, except where the circumstances do not exclude the possibility of assistance to the enemy being intended by the person so leaving Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It seems to
me unnecessary to go into all this. It is now a criminal offence for a man who is under this prohibition to leave the country. As a general rule it is not an offence for a man to leave the country, but when we are at war an alien enemy commits an offence by leaving. If I assist him in committing an offence I become an accessory. What is the reason of all this enactment? I have sympathy with the object, but it seems to me that this is a useless piece of law-making.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think the
right hon. gentleman is quite correct in saying that if we say to an alien enemy: You are prohibited from going out of Canada, and if he goes out of Canada he commits an offence or crime. He does not commit an offence under the general criminal law. He is prohibited from leaving, and efforts are made to prevent him doing so and to retain him if he endeavours to leave. But I do not think it goes 771
so far as to make him a criminal. Those whom we have detained in this country under this prohibition are not detained as people who have committed a crime but as prisoners of war. There has been on their part no crime, and 'therefore those aiding or assisting them, cannot be accessories to the commission of a crime. We want to make it an offence under the criminal law to aid or assist any person such as mentioned to violate the prohibition imposed upon him.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3:
3. The following section is inserted immediately after section 357 :
357a. Any person who sells or agrees to sell land or any interest in land to which he knows he has not a good title free from encumbrance, and receives the purchase money or any part thereof and without lawful excuse does not apply the money so received by him in procuring a good title or in reduction or discharge of encumbrances against the said land or interest in land, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to three years' imprisonment.
2. Where such sale or agreement for sale is made by a body corporate, every director, officer, agent and employee of the company who knowingly takes part in any offence within the provisions of this section shall be liable to the penalty hereinbefore prescribed.

The Bill of the hon.
member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraneyj is very different from this provision. That Bill provided that the vendor receiving money for land should hold it in trust and apply it in obtaining a title, but I am afraid that this section goes to dangerous length. Let me read it:
Any person who sells or agrees to sell land or any interest in land to which he knows he has not a good title free from encumbrance, and receives the purchase money or any part thereof and without lawful excuse does not apply the money so received by him in procuring a good title or in reduction or discharge of encumbrances against the said land or interest in land, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to three years' imprisonment.
Perhaps I could illustrate my point by stating a case with which I am familiar. Take the case of a land company selling land against which there is an encumbrance. That company is very careful to keep enough money in reserve to make good the title when the vendor pays all that is due. But if anything should happen to the investment, no matter how careful the company might be, I am inclined to think that the directors would be liable to be sent to the penitentiary because they had not put all the money in the Government savings bank in order absolutely to do away witli

Uhe possibility of any loss. In the particular case of which I speak the purchasers of the land all know of the encumbrance. In this Bill no exception is made of a case in which the purchaser may know that there is an encumbrance upon the property. He might be paying by instalments, and might know that the title could not be obtained for a number of years; yet if anything should happen, the vendor would be criminally liable. I am afraid it goes too far. This section says:
If he receives the purchase money or any part thereof and without lawful excuse does not apply the money.
What would be a lawful excuse? Would it be that the original owner would not take the money-he is not obliged to take it within a certain term of years. Would that be a lawful excuse? I do not think it would be. I did not see the Bill until to-day, but I suggest to the Minister of Justice that it is worthy of very careful consideration before it is passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. member that the dispositions of .the proposed enactment certainly call for very careful consideration. I do not think that any of the members of the special committee that dealt with it were blind to the dangers that might be involved in passing this section. We endeavoured, however, to get at a formula which would reach those who are intended to be reached, and at all events to do as little injury as possible to anybody engaged in a legitimate business. In the case which the hon. member suggested, it would seem at first glance as though the [DOT] circumstances which he related would constitute a lawful excuse. But this is the evil that is sought to be got at-and perhaps that is the clearest way of explaining the purpose of this section. If its wording can be amended in order more absolutely to ensure the attainment of its purposes, and to make as remote as possible any injurious consequence to people doing a legitimate business, I certainly shall be glad to accept any suggestion in that direction. The class of people who are sought to he reached by this legislation are to be found in considerable numbers in the West-at all events their lands are there-and they are also to be found in eastern Canada. Most of the lands are in the more or less approximate neighbourhood of our great cities. What this class of man does is this: he goes out and gets a promise of sale, or, perhaps, a sale subject to a very large encumbrance, of a large tract of land, or he may get an

option upon it. He then subdivides that land into small lots, advertises them, takes people out to see them, gives the whole tract a beautiful name, submits a beautiful plan for its development, and proceeds to sell these small lots, taking a small payment down and the balance in instalments. In that way he disposes of a great number of lots, and when the monthly payments are all made the unfortunate purchaser asks for his title, only to find that the vendor himself can get no title, or, at all events, no clear title until he has made further large payments.
Why do the purchasers not look after their business properly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is to be admitted that this proposed legislation is to protect people who do not look after their business. If everybody looked after his business, there would be no justification for this legislation. But the class of people who have been made to suffer in this way may not unfairly be described as unable to look after their business; they do not understand these things. It is represented to me on credible authority that a large number of the victims of this kind of business are domestic servant girls and young men and women employed as clerks.
Will making the offence a crime minimize the possibility of its recurrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was hoped that the
people engaged in this kind of business, who managed to get the money out of these unfortunates and to keep themselves in a position of independence in respect of the execution of a judgment, might have some fear if they saw the penitentiary before them.
Would it not be a crime in any event for the vendor to dispose of the receipts for the money of the pur-cnasers and not apply that money to the liquidation of the securities against the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Morally, yes.
I did not mean morally.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that
there is any provision in the criminal law to cover that.
I should think that somewhere in the transaction there would be an element of fraud.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These gentlemen are very ingenious, and cover these things up. No doubt the transaction is utterly dishonest, but in the contract there is not any express stipulation that the one dollar or two dollars a week, or whatever it is, that is collected is to be immediately paid over; the business is not carried on in that way. I do not think that it can be suggested that you can find anything in the law to create a trust as regards.these moneys. There are provisions which make the diversion of trust funds a crime. As the Bill was originally introduced, it proceeded upon the line of declaring the existence of a trust when people received money in this particular way. In that form it seemed to be open to the objection that whether or not that constituted a trust was a matter of civil and not of criminal law. I dare say that this might have been adjusted by inserting a provision which would bring such an act under the section that makes a breach of trust a crime under certain circumstances, but it seemed more desirable to get at just the thing that was done, to say that it is an offence and to punish it. As I have said, this legislation is to take care of people who do not know how to take care of their own business. With regard to those who are able to take care of their own business they do not need protection, but I do not know that any evil can arise from our trying to protect the other by putting the terror of the penitentiary before persons who are engaged in operations of this kind.

Would it not be better to go to the provincial legislature and ask them to say that no such contract as the minister has described can legally take place without the intervention of a trustee, that is that the land should be conveyed to a trustee and all payments made to the trustee. You might prevent it in that way, but I do not think that this Bill will stop the offence.
What would be the minister's interpretation of the Words " lawful excuse "?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the committee we
went over that at considerable length, but we concluded that we might safely leave it to the court. For instance, one thing that would be a lawful excuse would be where the vendor of these small lots explained fully all the circumstances to the purchaser and the documents showed that the purchaser knew all about it and therefore was absolutely trusting the vendor, and when it
was shown that in using the money, not immediately applying it to the clearing of the title but using it otherwise, the vendor was acting in accordance with what was clearly understood by all parties to the transaction, he would have a lawful excuse; but to undertake to define all the circumstances that might constitute a lawful excuse would be a good deal of an undertaking. I propose to suggest the addition of some lines to make it more clear that in some cases a man not only has a lawful excuse, but may be justified.

Take a company which sets aside, bona fide, a reserve for the purpose of meeting the demands of the original owners, but through some misfortune, the failure of a bank or a trust company, the money is lost. By this you would have to send the directors to the penitentiary. Would that not be a lawful excuse?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would that not be a
case where they had not retained the actual money but had set aside a reserve of sufficient money to provide for the clearing of the title? I should think that would not be a question of lawful excuse, but a case where the parties did not do the thing contemplated by the statute. I hardly think that the court would give it such a Judaic interpretation as that.
Supposing that a company invested the money but the investment became less valuable or the money was lost, would that be a lawful excuse?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think the
statute would cover the case of the loss of money unless, being under obligation to apply it at once they had diverted the money to other purpose.

Would the minister
accept an amendment which would make the thing more clear?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would welcome it.

In many cases lands of this kind are purchased by corporations and companies. They have to pay officers, agents and commission; and certain expenses connected with the business, and the company is perhaps doing a good business. The land is being sold fairly rapidly and they have reasonable grounds to believe that they will be able to set aside enough to pay these owners; they then declare a reasonable dividend upon the shares of the company, even before the property is entirely paid for-and then things would go

bad as they have done in the West and in many places in the East. Would that be a lawful excuse? You will notice that the wording of the section is very strong:
And if he receives the purchase money or any part thereof and, without lawful excuse, does not apply the money so received.
That means if they do not apply the last $5 of that money towards either paying for the title or providing for the encumbrances, they come within the purview of the statute. My hon. friend beside me says they might have to pay taxes. I think anybody will admit that as a lawful excuse. But if they paid commissions or dealt even generously with themselves in paying dividends, what would the minister think about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It always comes back to this, whether they have retained sufficient money to meet these obligations. I do not take it to mean that we are going to follow the particular bills they get to see what they 'do with them, they might pay dividends if they had enough money at the time to meet their obligations. Then I think they would be perfectly justined in paying dividends and that would be a lawful excuse; that having made the profits they paid the dividends, always retaining enough to meet these obligations when they would be called upon to do so. But again I say I would welcome any suggestion that would enable us to make this law applicable to the dishonest handler of real estate and protect the honest one. While I have a sort of shared responsiblity, this particular clause is the child of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), and he succeeded in impressing it upon the special committee. This Bill carries out the idea of the Bill he introduced.

Not being a lawyer, I am somewhat diffident about entering into this particular discussion. It seems to me that the object -sought to be attained is to protect, shall I say the fool or the man who does not apply ordinary business principles to his transactions? This amendment, it seems to me, would do away with dealings in agreements of sale. You take an agreement that has passed through one, two, three or four hands, must each individual see that the money has been applied to the purpose of paying off somebody ahead of him? If any man would apply ordinary business methods and ordinary business sense in a transaction of this kind he would not find himself in a position such as is

sought to be covered here, that he cannot get title after he has paid the money, i ou cannot protect people who will not pay the ordinary reasonable attention to the business they are attempting to transact. I think myself this particular clause should be withdrawn from the Bill.

It seems to me one part of this Bill contradicts the other. Section 3 says:
Any person who sells or agrees to sell land or any Interest in land to which he knows he has not a good title free from encumbrance,-
That is perfectly clear. It must be a perfect title. A little further on it says:
-or in reduction or discharge of encumbrances against the said land.
I would like some explanation of the expression "good title." Can a title be good that is not free from encumbrances? I am inclined to think that we should not call that in French a bon titre.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What the section says is, not the man who has a good title free from encumbrance, but the man who has not a good title free from encumbrance. The Bill provides that when -a man has not a good title free from encumbrance the money must be applied to clearing off those encumbrances.

Supposing there was only a sale of equity in the property, and that it was never intended that the encumbrances should be discharged. Surely it would not be expected that -the vendor should apply all the money he receives towards reducing an encumbrance which he was never intended to release.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The section provides for the case of a person who sells or agrees to sell land; that is one case; and secondly, it provides for the case of a person who sells or agrees to sell any interest in land. That would cover the case of a man who sold the equity in land to which he knew he had not a good title when something remains to be done to perfect the title, and of course the man has no title at all. Fraud may be committed by a man without any title at all.
A man may sell his neighbour's property.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Such things have happened.

I think the Bill
is intended to cover a number of cases that

developed in the recent land boom in the West. I submit that to put legislation of this character on the statute book at this time would result in the blackmailing of many an honest man in the eastern provinces who has sold property in good faith. Take the conditions that exist in my own province. Under the system of registration of titles that we have down there, property frequently passes from one man to another without any searching of title. When a farmer sells some property to another farmer he passes the property by
10	p.m. deed and gets a conveyancer, not a lawyer, to do the work. He does not bother to go to the registration office in a great many cases. Suppose that it developed afterwards that some old encumbrance had been against the property seventeen or eighteen years before, and that no claim had ever been put forward in respect to it. The man who originally held the encumbrance might have died suddenly and his heirs or executors turn up and assert these encumbrances. There are various questions of equity and rights that might arise between the parties, and irrespective altogether of whether you could show a crime within this Act, look at the possibility of so many honest men being liable to be pilloried and brought before a criminal court in order to show that they had transferred the property in good faith. In my province, where I am actually engaged in the practice of the law, I could cite numerous cases to the minister where hardship would be done if you made it possible to bring before a criminal court every one of our honest people down there who have transferred property.
This is only against the man who .sells it knowingly.

That is not the question. We know that an honest man can defend himself and get justice from the jury if he goes into court; but the question is, should he be made liable to the danger of prosecution ? As I said, nine-tenths of the property transfers in our part of the country are made without any search of title. Titles are searched only by close business men, companies, and people generally engaged in business; but in the ordinary conveyance from man to man the title is not searched. In answer to my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), my objection is this: That you are putting it into, the hands of a purchaser to pillory a perfectly honest man and bring him before
a jury to prove that he did not know there was an encumbrance against the property he sold. Further, this legislation is simply locking the door after the steed is stolen, for the land boom in the West is over, and nowadays any man who buys property sees that he gets the goods before paying his money.

I agree with my hon. friend from Kootenay that this clause should be struck out. I do not believe in legislation of this character. I think the law as it stands to-day in most of the provinces, sufficiently protects purchasers. There is no reason why a person who wishes to buy a piece of property cannot find out exactly what encumbrances are against it, and protect himself before making his payments. I do not think this amendment to the code has received the consideration it should have received. I think that the Bill might very well stand over until next session. I do not say that it is altogether desirable, but undoubtedly a practice does prevail in different provinces throughout the country of dealing in agreements for sale of land. I think if this amendment to the code were carried it would be going very much farther than anybody in this House has any conception of, and for these reasons I am opposed to it.

I think if my hon. friend from Victoria looks into the matter, he will find that the law of the provinces does not provide an adequate remedy for purchasers. He will 9ee that there is absolutely no protection ait all against a vendor who has no financial responsibility. This Bill was introduced by me because of numerous cases which have come to my attention as a practising lawyer in my own province. My hon. friend, who is a lawyer, knows the remedies as well as I do. I will give a case that has come to my attention in which there is not element of fraud, and my hon. friend will see the necessity of making some provision in the law which will compel a vendor to apply the moneys that he has received the discharge of encumbrances.	.
Could you not do that by provincial legislation?

Under the law as it is at present, a man having paid for his land, or nearly paid for it, or who is ready to make his last payment, is entitled to sue for specific performance. In default of

specific performance he is entitled to a judgment for damages. He cannot get specific performance, and a judgment for damages is absolutely of no use to him. The provincial legislature cannot legislate any further than the voiding of the contract. It can impose no penalties which in future will be any terror to a man, or make him deal fairly, or prevent a repetition of what has already occurred. Here is a model case, and it is one of the best cases I have in mind: a party purchases 6,400 acres, or ten sections, of land. He sells a quarter-section at a considerable profit. He receives most of his money; the balance, I think in this particular case, was some $800. He came to me and said: I want you to see that I get title. When I came to go into the matter, I found that there were encumbrances to the extent of several thousand dol'ars against the 6,400 acres of which this 160 acres was only a small part, and that the money that had been paid in by my client had not been applied to the discharging of these encumbrances or to taking care of the title, hut had been used for other purposes altogether. I said there was no fraud as far as I knew.

If it had come before
the court how would you have advised him?

I would have advised him to give up the purchase altogether. But he did not come to me, and it is a good deal, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) points out, in our province as in his; these transactions are not conducted through solicitors. They are conducted largely between the parties themselves. While the hon. member for Pictou wants the law left in its present unsatisfactory condition because that practice prevails in his province, it is because that very practice prevails in my province that I want the law amended to protect these people. The other case which I wish to mention is that in which a school-teacher invested $1,500, which it had taken her some years to earn. She came to me too late; she cannot get her $1,500 and has no remedy, because the man who received the money spent it very foolishly. Had the law been that he should turn all the money in to clear up the land which he purported to sell, I am satisfied that he would have done it. As to the particular language of the section,
I have no choice. I wanted to get at the evil, and I drafted certain language. Perhaps my draft, in the view of, the committee, and having reference to what the minister has said, is along lines that could 
have been dealt with by provincial legislation. It might be wel for the provincial legislature to declare that moneys paid by a purchaser under such circumstances should be trust moneys, but while they do that they can impose no penalties of a criminal character.

I think the law should protect the confiding and unwary. I know of cases where money has been paid by purchasers to vendors, who, having promised to discharge certain encumbrances, have not done it. If we had a provision in the Criminal Code making them liable to imprisonment, we might have more honesty in the vendors of land.

About a year or two ago a number of men came from the West to the East selling land, and collecting large sums of money. When the purchasers asked for their deeds, they found that the sellers did not own the land at all. The men who came were men who represented companies with high - sounding names, some from the city of Toronto. An investigation was made by a great number of these people, representing some $10,000 in money, and they found that the company which was selling this land through agents never had spent one cent for the land. When the purchasers attempted to collect the money they found that the company had gone into liquidation. This is a case which this Act will meet. I think that this is good legislation and that men who do acts of that kind, and have been doing them all through the maritime provinces, should be punished. Of course, the public were foolish in paying out their money to - men whom they did not know and without making an investigation as to title; but the unsuspecting public will always exist. 1 think this protection should be retroactive. It should have been on the statute book before. During the boom in the West hundreds of thousands of dollars have been paid by people in the maritime provinces to irresponsible men and there have been no returns.
I wish to ask the hon. Minister of Justice whether this legislation is retroactive and would apply to any transaction that has been entered into up to the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in the Act which makes it apply to what a man did before the Act was passed.

If that is the case, it is scarcely worth while enacting this legisla-

tion now, because, as a number of hon. members have remarked, the so-called boom and speculation in real estate has pretty well passed, and the damage has already been done. I noticed that the Minister of Justice, also the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and now the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I. (Mr. A. A. McLean), have made statements indicating that all the ill-advised speculation which has taken place in Canada during the past two years had taken place in the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought I gave the
East its fair share.

The minister may have
corrected himself later, but I think he referred to the western land boom. Then we have the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., saying that his friends down there were-I do not know whether he said robbed- *by people coming from western Canada. So far as speculation in western Canada is concerned, there has been a good deal of it bad, but a good deal of it good. I do not think there has been more speculation of a bad character in western Canada than there has been in eastern Canada. All the cities of Canada during the last few years have been engaged in wild speculation. The fever seems to be abroad, no matter whether you are in the East' or in the West. I would far sooner invest my money in land in the West than in the mines of Cobalt or in the foxfarming industry of Prince Edward Island, where I believe the companies even go so far as to sell the young foxes before they are born.
I was favourably impressed with this legislation when it was introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney). I saw the Bill, and I have kept conversant with its progress through the committee, although I was not a member of that committee. No one can deny that some necessity exists of protecting the people who have been or who may be wronged by real estate agents; but if you introduce legislation to protect people against real estate agents, you will have to introduce legislation to protect people against the fraudulent sale of other commodities than real estate. It is perhaps too much to ask an ordinary individual to consult a lawyer every time he buys a piece of property. That is all right from the lawyer's standpoint; but from the standpoint of the ordinary individual, it is too much trouble and expense. Some amendment might be put into the Bill which
would meet the case. For instance, if it could be shown that knowledge of the circumstances of the title had been given to any purchaser, there could be no complaint. This Bill will strike with some force, and perhaps do some injury to companies like colonization companies which have been doing good work in the colonization of western Canada within the past number of years, and which perhaps, when immigration begins again, will do some more good work.
As regards speculation in the East and in the West, the worst subdivisions that have been put on the market in western Canada-have been put on by men coming from eastern Canada and from the United States, but mostly by men from Ontario. The case at present going on in the Toronto police court, where five men were charged very recently, bears out my statement. If the assets or the resources of western Canada have been exploited to the injury of the people in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, that exploitation has been done very largely by people of eastern Canada and not by bona fide residents of western Canada,
They employ agents.

I do not know anything
about that. The worst subdivisions put on the market in Regina, Edmonton, Calgary or Saskatoon have been floated in England by men who have been dealt with in the columns of Toronto Saturday Night. With regard to this legislation, I cannot see any force in the words " without lawful excuse." What can a man give in court as a lawful excuse? The Minister of Justice says: we shall leave it to tne discretion of the judge in any particular case. What is the judge going to say? If I get money from a man to whom I have sold property and I put it into a bank in order to give it to the man from whom I have bought the property, and the bank fails, will that be a lawful excuse? If I put my money into a mortgage which was secure at the time, and which to-day has decreased in value and is not secure, will that be a lawful excuse? In view of the criticism that has been made of this measure to-night, it may be a very wise course to pursue to have the matter delayed for a short time until some amendment to the Bill can be considered.

Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the Special Committee to which this Bill was referred. Not having heard the discussion of a few moments ago in this Hduse I hope I shall not repeat something that has already been said. We experienced

a great deal of difficulty in regard to the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney); but as there was a general opinion that something should be done, the Bill was sent forward in this form. After a little further consideration of the Bill, I came to the conclusion that one weakness was just what the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) pointed out, namely, the indefinite meaning of the words " without lawful excuse." The next objection that I see to it is that it hits the honest man as well as the fakir-I say it without any disrespect-who is a real estate agent only in times of boom when he goes into the business because he sees other people making money. We have in Canada a number of reputable, established firms who have been engaged in the real estate business to the satisfaction of their clients and who have been honest in their dealings. It seems to me that the language of this section would hit them and prevent honest, fair dealing with the people, and in fact prevent proper expansion and development in time of need. Therefore, I would rather fall in with the suggestion of the hon. member for Regina and say that this House should take more time for consideration before putting upon the statute book a measure which may lead to consequences that are not immediately apparent. As it is rather a radical section, it should be worded so as to reach the man of criminal intent only.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In view of the new
proposal brought forward, I think this clause might with the consent of the committee be allowed to stand for further consideration.
On section 4-fraud, etc., in connection with sale, etc., of military stores:
Why are the provisions of this section made to apply merely to military, militia and naval stores? Why should they not apply to stores bought for any department of Government at any time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is another section introduced originally by a member of the House, one who, no doubt, was impressed with the necessity of giving at this time special protection in the case of purchases made for military and naval purposes. Whether it is desirable to extend this very special protection to cover all transactions with the' Government is a matter perhaps for some consideration. It is pointed out that we are giving very special protection here in making it a crime

to supply defective stores. I have no hesitation in saying that present conditions make it fairly clear that it would be wise to make this provision with regard to this particular kind of stores. These stores are bought in large quantities and in a great hurry and under circumstances.where it is not possible to proceed with all the care that might be taken in the case of other stores required in the normal condition of affairs. I am not saying that it is not desirable to extend this protection to all transactions with Government, but the proposal as it came to the committee dealt with naval and army stores, and it might as well be frankly admitted that the other subject did not occur to the committee. It is in any case not as pressing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-performing dramatic, etc., copyright works without consent of author:

Supposing that an amateur with some ability, in preparing for a church cohcert or something of that kind, strings together a number of popular airs from copyrighted operas and gives them in public, what would be the lesult?
Air. DOHERTY- The section coniines it to such performance? as are made f <r private profit.

I have a case in mind A person having more than usual ability as an amateur actress made a play of airs from c-i.rio. operas. If tile entertainment proved a success and it were taken to a neighbouring town, the party might be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two months. Would that be the effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If a person takes copyrighted property and uses it for private purposes, the mere fact that some charity gets a share of the profit would not relieve the party. This section reproduces the provisions of the English law on the subject and these provisions were in substance adopted in this House of Commons in 1909, at the instance of the Hon. Mr. Aylesworth, then Minister of Justice. I am not quite clear that there would be very great hardship in the case suggested by the hon. member. But it has been brought to our attention that there is really very great injustice caused and going unpunished under the law as it stands. We have had not a few instances of reproduction, purely for private profit, of dramatic masterpieces, the production of distinguished foreign authors, by utterly irresponsible people who have

managed to run them for a few weeks and make money out of them, and who, when a remedy was sought by recourse to the civil court, were found to be perfectly independent of any means at the disposal of those courts to compel them to indemnify the parties suffering. They were without assets get-atable and were irresponsible in every way, and the complainants found themselves in a position where they had no remedy. The matter was very forcibly brought before this House by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who moved a resolution which still stands on the Order Paper, and which was debated, but the debate adjourned. It commended itself to the members of the committee. There certainly is a wrong here without any adequate remedy. I have had communications that have made it clear to me that the continued existence of that wrong created an opinion among people in other countries whose opinion is worth something not over-favourable to our consideration in Canada for that sort of property which consists of the products of man's intellect.
Even if it should happen to operate in some way to embarrass people who want to use copyrighted productions for charitable purposes, I think that the evil to be remedied is greater than any evil which could arise under those circumstances.
I would call the minister's attention to the words " in whole or in part." The song introduced might be a single selection from a comic opera.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is a copyright on a single song it may or may not be worth anybody's while to protect it, but under our copyright law we have given to the author the right that no one shall reproduce it. It is true you may get it down to such a small point that it will not be worth complaining of, but we have recognized by law, under our own statutes, the right of a man to say that no one shall reproduce his copyrighted work. It seems to me that we ought to follow that up by giving adequate sanction to our own law: to make our own law respected.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 6 -penalty for being inmate of bawdy house:

Will the hon.
gentleman explain this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose is to
make possible the imposition of a longer
term of imprisonment upon persons who are found guilty of the offences here described. With regard to young girls who unfortunately find themselves inmates of institutions of this kind, under the law as it stands at present there is no means by which they can be placed under control and guidance and direction for a sufficiently long period of time to bring about a reformation.

What about the
Bon Pasteur institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bon Pasteur institution is a most excellent place, but under the law as it now stands a girl could not be committed there for more than three or four months-I have forgotten the exact period. It is sought to make it possible to send girls there for a year, so that if in the judgment of the magistrate the case is one in respect of which that period of time should be fixed, a long enough time may be provided to enable the reformative influences to produce an effective result. It has been pressed upon me strongly, not only by persons connected with tbo women s jail in Montreal and the institution referred to by the hon. member for Laval, but also by other people of, I might say, almost all the religious denominations who take an active interest in the, reformation of these unfortunate girls, that this proposed amendment would be a great improvement upon the law. This opinion is expressed not because there is a desire to see these children-because in many cases they are mere children-more severely punished, but because they see that what happens is this: these young girls who are sent in for a month or two months may develop good dispositions while they are there, but there is not time to bring them to that frame of mind where you can look for perseverance I have been told by perfectly credible people that in many cases the unfortunate experience of the matrons and those who are in charge of these jails is that they stand at the door as the young woman goes out after a couple of months and see her whisked off in the automobile of the proprietor of the house for being an inmate of which she was convicted. While this amendment, on its face, looks like the exercising of greater severity towards these unfortunate children, it can be made to operate as a very great assistance in bringing about the reform of young women of this class. It is made applicable even on first offence. That is done because it is pointed out by those who speak

from experience that if you reserve the application of such a provision for the second, third or fourth offence, you practically do away with the possibility of carrying out an effective reform.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-penalty for third, etc., convictions :
Section 228, referred to in this section, deals with the keeper, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; it makes a long term of imprisonment possible upon conviction for third or fourth offence.
Do you deal with the proprietors of houses in which such places are kept? They are the great source of complaint in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provisions which I laid before the House two sessions ago cover fairly well, I think, the matter of dealing with the proprietors of these houses.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Although I feel that
there is room for improvement in the law so far as it reaches or fails to reach the class of people sought to be reached by section 357 A which it was proposed to enact under section 3 of this Bill, I intend to move that section 3 be struck out. That does not mean that I would not give further consideration to the matter; I think that it certainly will require serious consideration, and if it be found desirable to proceed with it, it might be dealt with by another Bill. In any case, it is not desirable to retard the passing of these other amendments, which, I think, are all important. I beg to move, therefore, that the Bill be amended by striking out section 3 thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, during the last session and also since the beginning of the present ses fon-I moved for a full return of criminals found guilty and sentenced to capital punishment. That return I have now received. May I ask the Minister of Justice if he intends to have that return printed? It is most interesting and has required for its preparation a good deal of work on the part of the officers of the department. Besides, it proceeds on the same lines as a similar report published in England. I would not have a large number of copies printed, but [Mr. Doherty.j
I submit that it would be advisable to obtain a certain number of copies, to be distributed to the members of this House, the senators, the justices of various courts and to lawyers who would apply for it, in order that these various persons could be informed as to the development of crime in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think, it would certainly not be desirable to have such a return printed and distributed broadcast. It contains the names of persons who are still living but who have served their sentence and paid their debt to society. Such a report would be most injurious to them. I think it would not be well to make public a report that would draw public attention to the guilt of persons who are now leading an honest life.
It seems however that no objection could be taken to having a certain number of copies printed so long as we could control the distribution and limit it to the members of this House, the members of the Senate and the justices of the different courts.
As in the case of divorce proceedings, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When I have more time at my disposal, I shall gladly try to hand a copy of this report to all those who take an interest in the question. But I am anxious to prevent the circulation of such facts among people animated by mere curiosity, who might spread among the public data of a damaging and depressing (character.
