The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Department of Agriculture-Civil Government, salaries, $439,637.50.

I desire to secure some information about the regulations governing the shipping of potatoes. I presume that the-acting Minister of Agriculture (Hon. J. D. Reid) is not familiar with this matter and I would therefore ask that when his Estimates are next before the House he should have with him the official in charge of this matter. The regulations were passed on the 4th of November last and published In the Canada Gazette. They are simply impossible so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned; you might just as well pass a law that no potatoes should be shipped from the island.
MARCH 18, 191o

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has	called	my	attention to	this matter.The	regulations	were drawn	by the headof the botanist's department. Previous to that	there	was	an embargo	on potatoesgoing to the United States. In order to secure the admission of Canadian potatoes to the United States, the regulations of which the	hon.	member complains, were
drawn up by arrangement between the United States and Canada. Similar regulations are in force in the United States with respect to the shipment of potatoes.

These regulations apply
to any other province in Canada, not to the United States at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If you had not the same inspection for potatoes going to the other provinces we could not have secured the admission of any Canadian potatoes to the United States. The hon. member can see the necessity of having the regulations apply to shipments between provinces. Otherwise, potatoes might be shipped from New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island to Ontario, and from Ontario across the line.
But this prevents us from shipping potatoes to Nova Scotia or Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
There are no regulations to
prevent shipment between Prince Edward Island and 'Nova Scotia.

The regulations provide :
(b)	No infected potatoes shall be moved from the infected area within the Dominion of Canada to or through any other province outside this area, nor to any British or foreign country, territory or district thereof.
(c)	It shall be illegal to sell, offer for sale, dispose of in any way, receive or use, for seed, any potatoes affected with powdery scab.
3. Concerning movement of disease-free potatoes from the infected area.
(a)	No potatoes may be offered for shipment to or through the disease-free area unless the invoice is accompanied by an original certificate, and unless each container is plainly labelled as provided hereafter, and bears a copy certificate stating that the potatoes:
(b)	labeled " first grade potatoes " are of clean stock, were grown from clean seed and in soil not infected with powdery scab or any disease similar to powdery scab, and have not been in contact with any material, container or implement, through which they might have become infected with powdery scab and that have been inspected by an officer of this department before being offered for shipment and have been found free from powdery scab.
And then it goes on:
(c)	Persons intending to ship potatoes should apply for inspection thereof at least five days
in advance of the date of shipment, provided that persons using warehouses from which shipments are being made every third day or oftener, may request continuous inspection service, subject to special arrangements as to days when inspection shall be made. Each application shall state where the potatoes are located, their aproximate quantity and the expected date of loading. Forms of application for inspection will be furnished by the Dominion Botanist.
The bulk of the potatoes from Prince Edward Island are shipped in sailing vessels, which are engaged by wire, either telephone or telegraph. The season for shipping is very short and loading has to begin the day the vessel is chartered, because only a few days are allowed for loading and discharging. It would be almost impossible to give five days' notice to an inspector, because generally you would not know when you were going to get a vessel; you have to take your chance.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Let me give my hon.
friend my understanding of these regulations. The provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are not within the infected area of powdery scab, but everything west of the province of Quebec comes within the regulations that my hon. friend has just read. It was impossible for the Department of Agriculture to get the United States to raise their embargo on the shipment of Canadian potatoes unless we agreed to joint regulations, and their head botanist and the botanist for the Department of Agriculture got together and made joint regulations.
I can understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is where the line was drawn. Our representative was anxious to include the whole of Canada, but they drew .the line at the province of Quebec, and we had to agree to that. The hon. member will see therefore that there is no embargo at all n, so far as. shipments from Prince Edward Island and the provinces east of the Quebec boundary are concerned, but so far as west of that line is concerned, the regulations apply.

One of the officers who was inspecting on the island last fall held a different view. He may have been wrong, but he told me, when we were shipping potatoes to Nova Scotia, tuat we were liable to a fine unless we had tnem inspected. To inspect all the potatoes shipped would require at least one hundred inspectors in

that province. If the facts are as the minister has stated, that removes most of the c.ifficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
This matter came up only
a few days ago in connection with the trouble we had over a shipment to Boston. The position was explained to me then, and the deputy minister tells me now, that the explanation I have just given is perfectly correct. The regulations speak for themselves he says, and if the official in Prince Edward Island interpreted the regulations differently he was in the wrong.
Is the embargo still on shipments of potatoes from Canada to the United States? Is there anything new?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
It is still on; there is
nothing new.

Is there an embargo on the shipment of live stock, more
11	p.m. particularly horses, from Canada to the United States?'

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: As L understand it, an embargo has been placed on horses suitable for war purposes. If I recollect aright, horses between the ages of four and nine, or perhaps eleven, are not allowed to be exported if suitable for army purposes, but any horses between those ages that are unsuitable can be exported. I think the buyers do not take gray horses, horses with blemishes, or very valuable horses. Horses under or above the ages I have mentioned are allowed to be exported.

Does the Government
undertake to purchase from the farmers all the horses which are not allowed to be exported?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I could not answer that.
That would be a question for the Minister of Militia.

The reason I ask is
that in my opinion the reason we have ministers in different departments is that the minister representing a particular class in the Dominion can look after the interest of that class when questions affecting them come up. This is a very serious matter to the farmers of this country, they are placed at a very serious disadvantage if they are not allowed to export their horses to the United States. Hay is at a very high price, and the scarcity of feed in the West makes it almost an impossibility to feed tiie stock.
I heard the other day of a number of farmers in the Eastern Townships who

had actually sold their horses, or were desirous of selling them, because they could not very well keep them during the winter, and they were told that they would not be allowed to send them out of the country, and that if they attempted to do so the customs officials at the border would send them back. That is a very great hardship. It seems to me that it is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture to look after the interests of the farmers, and to know whether a market is being provided by the Government for these horses which the farmers are prevented from sending out of the country. The Minister of Agriculture should inform himself upon that point, and should let it be known, so that the farmers will understand the position in which they are in regard to horses, which are suitable for military purposes. I am told-I do not know how true it is-the acting Minister of Agriculture probably has informed himself or will inform himself upon the matter-that a very considerable degree of discrimination has been made between farmers, as to which side of politics they are on. I am told that - buyers of horses do not treat with equal favour Liberals and Conservatives. I have been told that in one locality, at all events, owners of horses had been given cards, which they could present to the purchasing agents, to indicate that they were of the right political stripe, and that it would be proper to buy their horses. That is not right. There should be no discrimination, and if the Government forbids farmers finding a market for their horses, the Government ought to be prepared to take these horses at a fair and reasonable price.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: This embargo was placed on horses by the Government for the reason that the British Government asked us to do so. Embargo was placed on many things, and amongst others on horses, in order that they might have a sufficient number for the war.

Was or was not that before the British Government began buying in the United States, and is it not a fact that the agents of the Government are making purchases of horses in the United States in very large numbers and that these horses are being shipped through United States ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Let me first answer the remarks of my hon. friend in reference to Canadian horses. This Government is purchasing in the several provinces a large

number of horses for use at the front. When a person wishes to export horses to the United States, and he brings it to the attention of the Government, the horses are allowed to go if they are outside of the embargo. If any person wishes to sell horses in this country, there is no trouble selling them either to this Government or to the British Government. The British Government have bought a great many horses in Canada and are continuing buying at the present time. I can hardly credit the statement of the hon. member, that a practice such as he suggests is carried on, although he states that he has heard of it. I do not know whether he knows it to be the fact.

You have not been in
Nova Scotia, especially in Kings county.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
It may possibly be. There
may be some person doing a thing of that kind, but I would hardly think that in the time of war any man would be guilty of such a thing.
That is what astonishes the people, because they say that when their boys go to the front they are not asked whether they are Liberals or Conservatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Horses are being purchased
in Canada by the Canadian Government, the British Government, and I think by the French Government. It is true they did buy a lot of horses, and perhaps are buying them now, in the United States, but I think the British Government, for a time after the outbreak of war, were anxious to get as many horses as they could from the United States, fearing that the United States Government might place an embargo on horses.
They have been buying here, and, from information I have, I believe they will take all the horses we have in Canada that are suitable for war purposes. The information I have received within the last few days, is, that all horses suitable for war purposes will be taken either by the Canadian Government, the British Government, or the French Government. The hon. gentleman referred to shipping the horses from United States ports. I should say that probably 80,000 or 100,000 horses have been shipped by Canadian ports. It is true they did ship a good many during the winter months by the United States. It was just before the foot and mouth disease broke out on the other side of the line, and it was considered very serious to allow the horses to come
through the states in which an embargo had been placed on cattle. There was a time when horses were diverted to the United States, but we did our best to get over that and, we succeeded in making an arrangement with the railway companies to have the cars disinfected at the border and brought in through Canada, so that the horses might be shipped through Canadian ports.

How is it that the shipment of Canadian horses through the port of St. John was suddenly discontinued two or three months ago? The question of the foot and mouth disease would not aSect that. I was in Boston not long ago, and I read in the newspapers that in one week four steamers left the port of Boston largely filled with Canadian horses. When the shipment of horses was started at St. John, a great deal of credit was given by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) in the Conservative papers for the favour that he was bestowing upon the port of St. John, for having the shipments of horses go through that port. Suddenly the shipments stopped through the port of St. John. Why have the shipments of Canadian horses through the port of St. John been stopped, and why have Canadian horses been shipped through United States ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I have not heard of any Canadian horses being shipped through American ports, although my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major General Hughes) and General Benson would know more about that.
The Boston papers announced it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: They may have.
Does the minister know that Canadian horses have been shipped through Canadian ports to England during the past two or three months?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: For the British Government?
For the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
There were two difficulties in connection with the shipment of horses through St. John and Halifax. During the last two or three months there has been great difficulty in getting tonnage from either St. John or Halifax. We could not ship oats, hay, or other products from Canada for that reason, and we sent a special representative over to the old country to try to arrange for tonnage. I think the Prime Minister stated in the

House a few days ago that that representative had arranged for two or three vessels a week, or otherwise we could not get anything away from our ports. The hon. member knows that all winter we have beSn shipping all the oats and hay we could via St. John. General Benson had difficulty in shipping horses from St. John, but he could get tonnage via the United States, and that is the reason why he shipped them that way. There was also some question about the difference in time between shipping from Montreal and shipping from New York or Boston.
What about St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The tonnage could not be got, and it takes eight or ten hours longer to ship that way. In the cold winter months that length of time would affect the horses on the cars.

General Benson ought to be reprimanded by this Government. I understood that he, or some one acting under him, stated on the train that St. John or Halifax, particularly St. John, was not a suitable port from Which to ship horses and live stock, and that therefore it was better to go to Boston. That is the rumour. I am afraid the hon. minister has not been quite frank with us to-night. First he told us that he did not know of Canadian horses having been shipped through American ports. Now he proceeds to tell us the reason why horses could not be shipped through Canadian ports, namely, the difficulty of getting tonnage. That is not the explanation given by that official. As regards St. John particularly, it was explained that, by reason of the rise and fall of the tide, it was not a suitable place from which to ship horses, and we were informed a few weeks before the shipments stopped that they were going to stop. A little bit of reasoning with the British officer would have informed him and clearly convinced him that there was no better port in America from which to ship horses or cattle than the port of St. John. The rise and fall of the tide adds to the convenience of shipping live stock, because they can be walked aboard the steamer without having to be lowered in slings into the holds of the "vessels, as is the case in ports where there is no such rise and fall of the tide. This officer did not seem to be aware of that fact, and I think it is due to the people of this country that some explanation should be given by the minister of the reason why Canadian horses during the greater part of this winter have

been shipped through American instead of Canadian ports. The country is going very properly to a large expense in equipping Canadian ports so that we may have traffic through them to as large an extent as possible both in summer and in winter. To me, as representing the city of St. John, it was a matter of great disappointment when I learned that a reflection had been cast upon our port, and that thereafter horses for Great Britain were to be shipped through American ports. Some explanation should be given to the committee and to the country as to why that has happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman states that he saw that statement in some newspaper. I can hardly credit the accuracy of the report. General Benson was born in Canada and has lived here most of his life. He is interested in Canada and is anxious to do everything he can in the interests of Canada. I know General Benson's views, and I am satisfied that he wants to ship everything from St. John or Halifax.

Could the minister tell us what number of Canadian horses have been purchased in Canada for the British Government, and how many have been shipped frotn Canada during the last five or six months, and through What ports they have been shipped? I may be mistaken, but I was informed by a gentleman in whose word I have confidence that what I have stated was the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If we are on the Estimates of Agriculture to-morrow, I will have that information. I had some information from General Benson; but I would not like to give the figures to-night, because I might be mistaken. I think the hon, member will be greatly surprised at the large number of horses that have been shipped through Canadian ports. If he will let the matter stand, I will promise to have the information, if possible to-morrow, and if not to-morrow, on Tuesday, by which time I can communicate with General Benson.

In connection with the number of horses purchased in Canada, a question of importance to Canadian horse buyers and breeders arises. In Montreal, all last fall an extensive buyer was importing wild, range horses from the southwestern States, and perhaps the same thing went on in St. John. He would bring in 500 horses, fifty of which might die in Montreal and fifty of which would not

pass inspection. The people are curious to know how the Customs Department handled those 100 horses that were missing; and how they cleared the bonds on 500 horses going out. In all parts of the country, people will point to a horse that has been bought very cheaply, and they will say. This is the Yankee horse that was refused in Montreal. I am sure the minister will be just as much interested as any one in getting at the bottom of that business. The Government was suspicious of this method of doing business, and at one time it stopped the importation and sale of those horses altogether. Maybe, that prohibition is still on. At the very time those horses were being imported, we were told that they were dying of pinkeye an Montreal. At the time that they were coming through in bond and being inspected in Montreal, there was an embargo on horse trading between Canada and the United States. This worked so harshly against Canadian farmers that the farmers along the boundary who sold cream across the line were compelled to hitch up a team of their own horses, haul the cream to the line, get it across the line the best way they could, and there hitch on another team of horses and go to the creamery, and then bring back the wagon and the empty cans to the boundary line and hitch on their own team again. The minister will have something to explain to the Canadian farmers as to that method of doing business, because there was not a little dissatisfaction as to those horses coming in. Yesterday I met a horse buyer, a good Conservative and a good horse dealer, who sold quite a number of horses last fall to those who were buying remounts, and he said to me very frankly:	The only place I can sell
horses now is in the United States; They are going into Massachusetts and Maine. I was not curious enough to ask why they were going into Maine, but the statement of the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) explains: they were going to Boston and Portland to be shipped.
From what part of the United States did those horses come, that were brought into Montreal?
They were range horses coming from points like St. Louis, Mo. They were altogether unsuitable for farm horses, and I understood that in Montreal they had a man who halter-broke and saddle-broke them.
Were they suitable for remounts?
They were purchased for remounts.
It is strange that horses of that kind should be brought in here for sale at the same time that horses were going from here to the United States to be sold for remounts.
Yet it is absolutely correct. The statement was made by a supporter of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Robb) is referring to horses purchased by General Benson or members of his staff for the British Government. No horses were purchased by any one in the United States for the Canadian Government. Some horses purchased by General Benson and his staff were brought to Toronto and Montreal for shipment through Canada to Great Britain.
This was at a time when the farmers were prohibited from crossing the line with their horses.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The horses bought by General Benson and his sta(| were brought to Toronto and Montreal and taken to the stockyards, and probably broken as the hon. member stated. It would be a very serious matter for our railroads and for the ports of Halifax and St. John if we had prohibited these horses from passing through Canada. I think the hon. gentleman will agree that the Government were acting rightly in allowing these horses to go through Canada.
How about the farmers crossing with their horses?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I was coming to that point. I remember a case and probably this will answer the hon. member. A shipment of horses, about five or six hundred, came into Toronto. They were from Kentucky, Illinois or some neighbouring state. They were brought there to be sold and shipped through in bond. When the inspectors in Toronto inspected them they rejected about sixty or a hundred horses. The question came up before me at the time. The parties who had the horses wanted to know if they would have to pay -duty oil them or whether they would be allowed to re-export them. Some of these horses were kept here and on these they paid duty. On any that were sent back to the United States no duty was collected. What was done in Toronto, I suppose would apply to Montreal.



The hon. member mentioned about farmers having to drive to the line and there change horses. Then that embargo was placed on horses on account of the foot and mouth disease, the orders of the Customs Department were issued accordingly to prevent it as the hon. gentleman has stated. That came up before me at the instance of those who lived near the boundary lines, and so far as the Customs and also the Department of Agriculture were concerned, as soon as it was called to attention provision was made for driving backwards and forwards without difficulty. I do not know whether people in the hon. gentleman's locality brought it to attention or not, but where the matter was called to attention the necessary provision was made.

My county is on the
boundary, and when the effect of this embargo was brought before the minister the matter was regulated without delay. The present Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) was also acting Minister of Agriculture at the time. An arrangement was made by which a person in New Brunswick who wished to drive into the state of Maine was allowed to do so, but was not allowed to put his horse into a stable-I think that was the provision; however, the difficulty was overcome. I never could understand why it was necessary to prevent the exportation of our horses to the United States. I know that it is because the war is on and the British Empire may possibly require these horses. But, from the very beginning the British Government were buying horses in the United States for the very same purpose for which we were holding them in Canada. It certainly works injustice in some places. Take my own county, for instance. I received a letter from a person representing General Benson, I suppose, asking if there were horses for sale in my part of the country. I replied, giving the names of many people who had horses for sale, including one firm of railway contractors that had thirty or forty horses stored in my town. They were perhaps heavy for remounts, but they would be splendid horses for artillery purposes. But nobody came to look at them, and I believe that not more than three or four horses were sold for these purposes from the whole St. John valley, which is the greatest horse-producing portion of the maritime provinces. The hon. member for Kings, N.S. (Mr. A. De Witt Foster), was not there; his activities were confined to Nova Scotia. I quite realize the ground on
fllr. J. D. Reid. 4
which the Order in Council was based, but I never could understand its desirability. Has not the minister made up his mind that it was not well advised, and might it not be rescinded?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The Order in Council was
passed at the request of the British Government. I do not think it was ill-advised. I feel that we shall require all the horses that are in Canada. While the Order in Council may be a hardship to some who have horses to sell, in the end, I am confident, they will suffer no loss, because there is going to be a demand that will take every horse in Canada.

I could mention politicians, supporters of the Government, in Carleton county, supporters of the Government who will buy horses quite as well as the hon. member for Kings, N.S., but I would not give them carte blanche, as the hon. member was given.

I should like to get also the number of Canadian remounts bought by General Benson and his staff in the province of Alberta. Thousands of horses can be bought in the province of Alberta to-day for military purposes at prices around $100 each. The Canadian Remount Commission are advertising in certain places for the purchase of horses, but the experience is that they pick up ten or fifteen horses at some important centre, Edmonton, for instance, where thousands of horses could be obtained. In the northern section of the province of Alberta large numbers of horses could be supplied for military purposes, and there is no possibility of selling them.

I have a very
.serious complaint to make about this horse-buying business; I was rather under the impression that we should bring this matter up when the Minister of Militia is present.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is just what I was going to say. The purchase of horses really comes under the Militia Department.

The Minister of Militia
is the man I was waiting for.

What is the use of
having a Minister of Agriculture in the Government if he does not look after the interests of the farmers? That is what he is in the Government for.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I really think the Minister
of Militia is the man who should answer

these questions. I may say to the hon. member for Mrathcona that I do not see how I can get the information from General Benson, but I shall be glad to get it if I can. So far as the purchase of horses is concerned, although I feel that that is a matter which comes under the Militia Department, I will try to give that information when the Agriculture Estimates come up again.
Mr. TuiilN: So far as my county is concerned, I have a complaint to make to the Department of Agriculture, in respect to horses. There is a gentleman in my county, a horse-buyer who ships quite a number of horses to the United States, and he asked me if there was such an Order in Council passed as that to which reference has been made. He wanted to ship some horses to the United States, and he pointed out that this Order in Council would be a hardship on the farmers. He said that the Militia Department had advertised to buy horses in the county on a certain date and that upon that date the farmers brought their horses in for sale, but nobody showed up to purchase. Subsequently the representatives of the department came to buy horses, when nobody knew they were coming. After receiving this information I put the following question on the Order Paper:
Has an Order in Council been passed prohibiting the sale and export to the United States
of Canadian-bred horses from four to eleven years old? It so, when was such Order in Council passed?
The answer given by the Acting Minister of Agriculture was as follows:
An Order in Council was passed on August 7, 1914, which prohibits exports to any place other than the United Kingdom or any British
possession of " saddle, draught and pack animals, suitable for use in war."
I should like to ask the minister whether this Order in Council compels people trading in horses to sell them to the Militia Department? Many horses which are bred in the Eastern Townships would bring from $300 to $500 if sent to the United States. A farmer who has a fine driver does not wish to sell it for $175 or $180 to the War Department. Would the hon. minister give me some information concerning this regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I have explained that this
embargo was requested by the British Government. Horses may be sold in Canada to other persons than agents of the Militia Department as a matter of course. If any person in the country represented by the hon. gentleman has a valuable horse that 78*
he wishes to sell or to export to the United States, all he has to do is to advise the Customs Department that he has for sale a horse that is not suitable for military. purposes, being, perhaps, too valuable; and the Department of Agriculture will have one of its officers examine the animal to ascertain whether or not it is suitable for military purposes. The British Government are only too .anxious to get all the horses they possibly can. If upon examination it is found that it is too valuable to be purchased for use by the Militia Department, the Customs Department will not prevent the exportation of the horse to the United States. When it was arranged that we should take up the Estimates to-night, 1 thought that we would go into Committee at about half-past nine. I did not intend to ask the Committee to sit later than eleven or eleven-thirty. If there is no objection, I suggest that we take up the vote for patent records. It is the same vote as last year; I suggest that we pass this item to-night; any discussion which may be desired upon this or any other item may be taken up when the Estimates come up again.
Patent records, $30,000.

Can the hon. minister
who is representing the Minister of Agriculture give us any information in connection with the patent for slyeld and shovel which was obtained from the Department of Agriculture by a young lady, Miss MacAdam, I think,? The hon. minister has already given me an answer to this question, but it is incomplete. That patent was obtained on August 17, 1914. I understand that a rush order was put through for that patent, over the heads of a great many other patents which were pending. Can the acting minister tell us, first, who was the inventor of the shovel? Was it the young lady herself, or did she obtain the patent for some other person? Second, who was it that asked that this rush order be put through? The answer given me on February 25 states that one of the reasons for the rush order was that the invention was required for use in connection with the war.
I cannot understand why it was absolutely necessary for this particular patented article to be used for military purposes. I should think that the Government would have a right to use it for military purposes even if it was not patented.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Then you would have to pay a royalty.
Not for military purposes, the Act is express in that.

I. understand that there is a clause in the Patent Act which says that no royalty need be paid and whether a royalty was paid is a question that could be better answered by the Minister of Militia. I would be anxious to find out exactly why a rush order was put through, at whose request and who is the inventor [DOT]of the shovel and shield in question.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Was not that information
given in the answer?

The patentee was given
but not the inventor.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I could not give the hon.
gentleman any further information than has been brought down. The application was made by the party named on the form necessary to obtain a patent. Whatever that form required was filled in by the party applying for the patent.
That form must be in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Unless I was given notice
I would not have the information before me.

The deputy minister
would have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He could not remember.

He would remember
this, it was a special matter, patenting a hole in a shovel. It is a pretty special sort of patent.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The hon. member has asked me for considerable information with reference to that patent. As I have stated, if he will let the rest of the discussion stand until our Estimates come up again I shall be in a better position to give information.

I have no doubt the
deputy minister could give the information.

In the answer given on the 25th of February it is said that the request for the rush order was given by the Deputy Minister of Agriculture to the examiner of patents. The deputy minister must certainly remember something.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The hon. member will understand that if any patent was applied for that would help the Militia Department in connection with the war it would hardly be necessary to ask the deputy minister to rush it through because he would do so in the public interest.
fMr. J. D. Reid.l

If the Government wanted to use this article for purposes of war it would not matter whether it was patented or not, and if the party afterwards got a patent it would be only a question of fixing the royalty and paying it. The question of whether the Militia Department wished to use the article or not plays no part in the matter. There must be some other reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think the hon. member could argue in the opposite way if necessary. Supposing a person had an article that the Militia Department wished to use, i-t would not be only fair that the Department should help to get the article patented so long as it would not cost the Militia Department any royalty, for the reason that some one else might obtain a patent on the article.
It does not make any difference, because the Militia Department have the right to use the article, patent or no patent.

I cannot see the line of argument of hon. gentlemen opposite. A certain article is invented by some person to be used for war purposes, and some one else desires to get a patent on the article. What is the objection to his getting a patent?
None whatever.

The hon. gentleman seems to argue that there is something wrong in getting the patent, so far as the Militia Department is concerned. That does not cut any figure because they can use it anyway; but other countries could not use it and any one interested in the article, for that person's own protection, might desire to get a patent in order to dispose of it to some other country. If it was to be used for war purposes, what was wrong about having the patent take precedence of others?

The hon. member for Frontenac is a good lawyer for a layman. Probably he does not remember that the mere fact that the Militia Department used this or any other article would not affect the right of the party to obtain a patent so long as it had not been on sale for more than a year in Canada or any other country prior to making the application. So that argument falls to the ground.
Is the minister sure there will not be any claim made by Miss MacAdam for the royalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That has been stated by the Minister of Militia.

One thing might be cleared up in regard to the matter; there is a great deal of doubt as to whether Miss MacAdam was the inventor of the patented article in question. She could not have got the patent unless she either swore she was the inventor or produced an assignment from the inventor.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
She swore she was the -[DOT]
inventor, and that is all the department could ask.

Could the minister, as a member of the Government dealing with this patent, tell me whether or not officials of the department thought that that particular invention was patentable? Was there a special order of the minister that the patent should issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There was no special order of the minister, it was all done by the deputy minister. The minister knew nothing about the patent; it never came before him at all.
What was the reason that the deputy minister made the order?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I have stated that these orders are given from time to time. This is not a special case. It is a practice of the department to give special orders.

Was there anything
about the patented article which required that it should be manufactured in the United States which necessitated the giving of an order immediately for 25,000 of these shovels with the hole in them, the patented shovel, to the Midvale Company in the United States, or could they have been manufactured in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think it is hardly fair for trie hon. member to press that question against me. All the Department of Agriculture has to do is to see that the departmental regulations regarding patents are observed.

Perhaps I can come to the rescue of the minister. A clause of our Patent Act, I think section 44, provides that the applicant upon application may be granted the privilege, under certain conditions, of not manufacturing in Canada. That is what is called the license clause. It was very important that this article should be manufactured at that particular moment.
Mr. ,T. J. HUGHES: What object had Miss MacAdam in rushing the application for the patent, if she was not going to get a royalty on the article?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If my hon. friend asks Miss MacAdam, he may get that, information.
Can the minister tell us whether this shovel had been patented in the United States prior to the patent being granted here, or whether it has ever been patented in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I could not answer that question. I am informed by the deputy minister that, so far as the examiner could find, the article had not been patented in any country except Canada. I cannot give positive information on that point.
Just a moment ago I understood the minister to advise the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., to go to the Militia Department ~and inquire for Miss MacAdam.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I said Miss MacAdam was an employee of the Militia Department, and the only one who could give the information he asked for. I stated where she could be found.
What position does she occupy in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I could not say. She is a permanent employee, and the Civil Service list gives her position.

Some time ago I forwarded to the Department of Agriculture a petition signed by a number of the farmers of the township of Cleveland, in my county, which reads as follows:
The petition of the undersigned rate-payers and voters of the county of Richmond humbly
i-epresents:	. .	,	_
That, on the second day of August, 1914, a most severe and disastrous hail-storm passed over our farms and ruined our grain crop;
That it is important that next year the farmers of this country should raise much more grain than ever before, on account of the war reducing the production and increasing the consumption of grains.
That your petitioners, in many cases, will be unable to do this on account of the high prices of seed grain.
That assistance by way of grants of seed grain in being tendered to the farmers of the province of Saskatchewan;
Now, therefore, we your petitioners, humbly request you to use your best efforts with our Governments, Federal and Provincial, to obtain for us a grant of seed grain to replace what we lost in said hail storm.
And you will do justice.

Signed at the said county of Richmond, this month of January, one thousand nine hundred and fifteen.
Adrien Thibeault.
This is signed by 75 or 80 farmers living in the township. The petition was forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture, who sent me the following letter, dated February 9 :
Dear sir,-I have your letter of the 2nd inst., enclosing a petition signed by Mr. Adrien Thibeault and others in the township of Cleveland, in the county of Richmond, praying that the Government supply them with seed grain for the loss they sustained in a storm which passed over that township last summer, and I note that you strongly endorse the same.
In reply I may say that the Honourable the Minister of the Interior is attending to the question of supplying seed grain in the West and I do not know that anything outside of the province of Alberta and Saskatchewan is contemplated. However, I am sending your letter on to the Honourable Dr. Roche for consideration.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) M. Burrell.
It was very little satisfaction for the farmers of the county of Richmond to be told that the petition would be referred to the Department of the Interior. Some of those farmers are in very poor 12 midnight, circumstances, and as the Department of Agriculture is at the present time sending gentlemen all through the country urging the farmers to greater production, it was not much comfort for those farmers who suffered great loss by the hailstorm, to be told that the petition was 'being forwarded to the Department of the Interior. I had this very nice letter from Hon. Mr. Roche, dated February 15:
My dear sir,-Your communication under date Of the 2nd addressed to the Hon. Martin Burrell with petition signed by a number of persons in the township of Cleveland, county of Richmond, province of Quebec, praying to be supplied with seed, grain, has been forwarded here.
In reply I beg to say that we are not having any distribution of seed grain in the provinces that own their natural resources. This is a provincial matter and although we have had applications from British Columbia, Ontario, and this one from Quebec we have referred them to their respective provincial Governments for assistance. We are only granting aid in the drouth stricken areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta to farmers who were deprived of their entire crops last year, and other such adjacent districts that have suffered from drouth and the farmers of which are in a similar position, the provincial governments promising to pass legislation to give our liens a priority over existing mortgages.
Yours faithfully,
W. J. Roche.
E. W. Tobin, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
What has that to do with patents ?
Have you been sleeping " I will send for the Minister of Justice to take care of you.
I think the hon. member is talking in his sleep. He is talking about something quite irrelevent to the item under discussion.
I think the hon. member-
I rise to a point ol order. I say the hon. member is not discussing the item before the House.
As I understood it, a general discussion was to be allowed on the item.
Oh, that must have been previous to my coming in. It is all right then.

The Minister of the Interim said in that letter that grain is not being distributed in those provinces which own their natural resources. I do not see why it should make any difference where the farmers. live, whether in the province of Quebec or in the West, so long as damage has been done to their crops, whether by drouth or by hail. I might read part of a letter that I received from a gentleman who forwarded me this petition:
He also feels positive that it is very important that these genuine sufferers should be aided this year, especially when there Is such great need for over-production by the farmers. The Agricultural Bureau, which you assisted to establish here, is conducting a campaign of " patriotism and bigger production " and something in the line of aid with seed grain will show by practical demonstration that the Government wants the farmers to do something to aid the Empire, while aiding themselves. The best assets our country can have is prosperous farmers and they cannot he prosperous the year after they have lost their crop of grain, unless they can get assistance with seed grain. You may safely tell the Minister of Agriculture that a short visit to the scene of this storm would have convinced him that there was need of aid to the sufferers. The West should not get all the favours.
Who signed that letter?

Mr. F. 0. Duboyce, notary public, Richmond, Quebec. Would the acting Minister of Agriculture grant the request" of these petitioners and send one of his men down to investigate, and if he finds that the case is a deserving one, will he give them some help?

I observe that the petitioners request the hon. gentleman not only

to approach this Government, but also to approach the Government of Quebec. Would he tell the committee the result of his application to the Government at Quebec in this connection?

This petition was sent to
me at Ottawa, and my first duty as representing the county of Richmond is to approach the Government here. I am a member of the House of Commons, and as such I am bringing this matter to the attention of this Government. The case of the farmers of Cleveland township is a just one. The Government are holding meetings throughout the country and urging farmers to produce more in order to help the Empire in this hour of trial. In helping these farmers they will not only be rendering a great service to the farmers themselves, but to the Empire as well. If the minister will send an agent from his department to Richmond, Mr. Duboyce, the notary public there, will arrange to have him taken out to the township of Cleveland.
Would my hon. friend inform me as to the date of the petition?
The second of February. It was addressed to the House of Commons, at Ottawa.
I understand the hon. gentleman has not approached the Quebec Government in reference to the matter.

In bringing this matter to
the attention of the minister I am simply doing my duty to my electors.

I understand that the
petitioners asked the hon. gentleman to approach both Governments.

I am not a member of the provincial house. I represent Richmond and Wolfe in the Dominion House. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture if he would be good enough to send a man from his department to investigate this claim which I have put forward on behalf of the farmers in the township of Cleveland. If he finds that the case as put forward is borne out by facts, will his department give help to these farmers and advance them seed grain in order to assist them in putting in their crops this spring?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
This is a matter that is being handled by the Department of the Interior, the reason being that the policy of assisting farmers in Alberta and Saskatchewan by the distribution of seed grain was started
in years gone by and is simply being continued. We are furnishing seed grain to farmers who are on land which is still the property of the Dominion Government. It is true, as the Minister of the Interior stated the other day, that the department has gone a little farther in these western provinces, by granting aid to persons occupying patented lands. I am not as familiar with the facts as my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior is; he will be on with his estimates to-morrow and will probably be able to answer the hon. gentleman's question more fully. With reference to the request of the hon. member that I send a man down to investigate this condition in his constituency, let me say that the petition that has been addressed to him, asks him, as the representative of those who have signed it, as their public servant, to come to this Government and see whether he could get them to take up the question of giving them aid. But dit goes farther; it asks him, as their representative, to go to the Quebec Government, if he does not succeed here, and request them to take cognizance of the difficulty they are in and to assist them in that locality. Having got a letter from my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) stating what the policy of this Government is, I think my hon. friend for Richmond and Wolfe was a little lax in his duty, if he had not time to go to Quebec, in not writing to Quebec and urging the Government there to take the matter up, he having failed in his effort at Ottawa. Perhaps that might have resulted in securing the aid required. At all events, he would have been carrying out the request of the petitioners. It is not too late yet; if he writes now, to-night, or to-morrow, to the Government at Quebec, and if they will take it up and deal with it, as I believe they should, the difficulty may be overcome. If the farmers in Cleveland township are in the difficulties stated by him, it is the duty of the provincial government to send a representative a. once and see that they are looked after and properly protected. Other provinces are in exactly the same position. We have had the same difficulty in Ontario. Hardly a year passes but a hail-storm or something else arises in certain parts of the province of Ontario, and people meet with disaster similar to that which has visited this part of the province of Quebec, and the representatives of the province of Ontario are told exactly the same thing, no matter what side of politics they are on. The same [DOT] answer is given to them as that

which was given to the hon. member who has just taken his seat. The Ontario Government cheerfully and willingly helps those who have been affected in this way in the province of Ontario.

So they do in
Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: So they do in Manitoba and in the other provinces. This opens up a very large question. We are carrying out the policy adopted by previous governments of assisting homesteaders on land owned by the Government, and we are at the same time protecting ourselves, in so far as the expenditure is concerned. It has been the opinion of all governments that the older provinces are able to look after their people who are in difficulty.

The minister states that this policy was inaugurated some years ago by a former Government to assist those people in western Canada who were homesteaders and who did not own their farms. He is following that up by assisting, not only homesteaders, but people in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan who own their land. On what principle does the minister assist a person in the province of Saskatchewan who owns his land, and whose crop has been hailed or who has lost his crop by drouth, and refuses to assist a person in the province of Quebec who owns his land and who has also been hailed out and has no seed grain?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That question was discussed a few days ago by hon. members from the West, when the hon. member was present, and the Minister of the Interior answered that question and gave the reason why. In the West the homesteaders are all newcomers; they have just received their patents, and the number is small.
A few thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Not very many in that particular district. If the hon. member is here to-morrow, I would like him to ask the Minister of Interior for the reason. The matter comes under his department. I feel that I am not justified in speaking for the Minister of Agriculture on a matter of this kind, because I am only acting temporarily.
I will not press the matter further.
The provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta passed laws giving the Government the prior right on mortgages in cases where it supplied seed grain.
They were asked to pass those law's. I have not heard that they have passed them.
Yes, they have passed them.
My first duty to my electors was to approach this Government, and I did so.	,
And you have not sue-ceeded.
I do not know. The minister has not said " no " yet. I may say that I wrote to my colleague in the local House and he has a copy of the petition,.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: How long ago is it since you wrote to him?

I did not mention any
(politics; I did not say that the people were Conservatives or Liberals. I am not speaking for the Liberals of the township of Cleveland alone, I am speaking for all the people who have lost their crops through the storms which passed-over that township in August last.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No one said that you mentioned any politics.
The hon. minister tried to make out a case against me.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.

The hon. minister said that in those provinces which he is helping, the land belongs to this Government. You must not compare the hardships of the earlier settlers in Ontario and Quebec who entered wooded land and had to clear it with the much happier position of the 'homesteaders on the western prairies, who simply had to plough the prairies and gather their crop. The pioneer settlers in the township of Cleveland had to go in there when there were no roads and no bridges, and they had to clear the land and spend $25 or $30 an acre in doing the work. They could not raise enough to keep them in those early days. They had to cut down the trees and burn and pull out the stumps. After doing all that work, they come to this Government for this assistance, and all the answer I get from the minister is that this Government does not ow'e anything to the people of Quebec. I am surprised that the hon. minister takes that stand. I hope the Hon. Walter Mitchell, who represents Richmond in the Provincial House, will have

more success with his Government than I have had with the Dominion Government.

I am sure the hon. .member has served the purpose for which he rose. He has represented his constituency and he has placed on Hansard his zeal in their behalf. If the principle he advocated were followed out by this Gov-eminent, every man from one end of Canada to the other who met with any loss, for instance, if his barns were burned down, would have a claim on this Government for assistance.
The case of Quebec or Ontario is different from that of the western provinces. In the West there was a general drouth affecting large sections of the country and people who had been in that country only a comparatively short time were absolutely dependent upon one thing, namely, upon the crop in the ground, which on account of the drouth realized absolutely nothing. That is not the case in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. In all those older provinces there is mixed farming and not simply the one crop of oats or' wheat on which the farmers are absolutely and wholly dependent. If the hon. member wants to be fair, he will admit that. Is he prepared to say from his place in the House now that he would uphold this or any other Government in acceding to the request of farmers in the older provinces for assistance every time they lost their crops through drouth or hail or some other cause? The hon. member was presented with a petition from his constituents as representing that county asking him to do two things, namely, to do a certain thing so far as this Government was concerned, and to do another thing so far as the Quebec Government was concerned. What did he do? He got the petition on the 2nd of February making the two requests. He comes here and finds fault with this' Government in very loud terms. He chastises this Government for lack of interest in the farmers of the province of Quebec. Every word he has said in censure of this Government can be applied to his own Government, in the province of Quebec. His words of censure also reflect back upon himself, because he has carried out only a part of the request made by the petitioners, that is, to apply to this Government. His first duty was to apply to the Provincial Government. He left that to a later date, because it would not serve his purpose, which was to make the application here. He is better pleased because it has been refused, because it places him in a position
of appearing before the people of the township as their champion and as a man ready to fight for their rights.

I do not think the hon. member is fair when he says my first duty was to write to the provincial government.
I got that petition. There was a copy sent to the member for the county of Richmond in the provincial government, and I also wrote to him. What was I to do? Was it not my duty, representing the county of Richmond and Wolfe in this House, to address myself to this Government?
Have the provincial government decided to do anything?

I could not say. But when the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) says that I should have risen in this House and- asked this Government, let me tell him that I have done so by letter to the Minister of Agriculture, and also by laying this matter before the House this evening. I did not mention any politics until the minister insinuated that this was a case of Liberals and Conservatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman misunderstood me.

I did not mean to refer to the minister. I speak of the hon. member for Frontenac:	When he tells me that it
was my duty to write to the provincial government, I say to my hon. friend that he is mistaken.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question?
Certainly.
Is not the representative of his county of the provincial House Provincial Treasurer of Quebec?
What has that to do with it?

It has a great deal to
do with it. The hon. member's colleague in the local legislature is a number of the provincial government. Surely, if he has any influence, he ought to he able to use it in a case like that. Yet he has apparently done nothing so far as his own province is concerned.

Here is a petition signed
by seventy-five to eighty farmers from the township of Cleveland, the people who have sent me here, asking me to take this up with the minister and to help the farmers to get seed grain. Was I to answer these

petitioners that they had no business to write to me, but that they should write to the provincial member? I am not trying to make politics out of this. I do not know whether these petitioners are Liberals or Conservatives-I hope they are all Liberals. But I do not draw any distinction, because when I am elected it is my duty to represent all. It is on those grounds that I was elected, and on those grounds I hope to be elected again if I am a candidate.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, the House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Friday.
Friday, March 19, 1915.
